title: Netflix announces 'Stranger Things' spin-off 'Other Worlds', and it's already teasing a trip to Area 51 (video)
content:
Netflix has announced a new live‑action prequel series titled “Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure.” The show is created by the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry, with episodes slated to be directed by Joe Wright, known for Darkest Hour and Black Mirror. Unlike the original series, the story is set in Marion, Nevada, in 1955, and the teaser trailer highlights a location that is unmistakably Area 51, showing a bike and radio outside a fenced‑in area marked as restricted.

No plot details have been released for the series. The teaser does, however, hint at a possible wormhole and features a date—April 19—on screen. Kate Trefry, who wrote the Stranger Things: The First Shadow play focused on Henry Creel, and Matt Duffer, who explained to Variety how the spin‑off would explore the rock Henry discovered in Stranger Things, suggest that the new series will center on Henry Creel and his journey toward becoming Vecna.

“Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure” is scheduled to debut on Netflix in 2028. The announcement follows Netflix’s continued expansion of the Stranger Things franchise, adding another chapter to the series’ lore.
summary: So, you thought "Stranger Things" was done and dusted after all that Conformity Gate nonsense? No way!
author: Space.com

title: Starfish Space Loses Contact With First Otter Spacecraft, Ending NASA Mission
content:
Starfish Space announced on Tuesday, November 3, that its first Otter spacecraft, Otter 24C, had lost contact and is not recoverable, ending the company’s NASA technology‑demonstration mission. The loss came after the satellite was only a month into its low‑Earth‑orbit (LEO) operations.

Otter 24C was launched on October 1 aboard SpaceX’s Transporter‑18 rideshare flight, which carried 130 payloads to LEO. Among those payloads was a prototype satellite for Google’s Project Suncatcher, an AI constellation. The Otter craft was participating in NASA’s Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY) mission, a program designed to demonstrate technologies needed for future debris‑removal operations and the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft. SSPICY’s goals include advancing NASA’s in‑space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) objectives to support a sustainable space environment and enable the assembly, repair, and maintenance of objects in orbit.

During commissioning, Starfish Space stopped receiving data from Otter 24C. An investigation revealed that a fault‑protection feature on the satellite bus, supplied by California company Astro Digital, triggered an error that disabled the radio and prevented re‑establishing communication. Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital concluded that the spacecraft is not recoverable. The company has said it is implementing fixes to reduce the likelihood of a similar issue in future missions.

Starfish Space emphasized that the work completed by Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of forthcoming Otter missions. The company continues to develop the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit. Meanwhile, its Otter Pup 2 prototype, launched in June 2025, has been approaching Gilmour Space’s ElaraSat and is preparing for a historic docking in LEO, marking the next step in the company’s servicing program.
summary: Starfish Space’s first Otter spacecraft, Otter 24C, lost contact in low Earth orbit after a glitch and was declared unrecoverable, ending the NASA Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY) technology demonstration mission that aimed to test debris‑removal and servicing capabilities. Otter 24C had been launched on Oct. 1 aboard SpaceX’s Transporter‑18 rideshare flight.
author: Space.com

title: Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman to develop TV series of Robopocalypse
content: They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation. It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay. That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required. But now we have been blessed with the news, first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords. "'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement. The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson Vintage The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson Vintage "Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together." As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping. The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," " The Andromeda Evolution," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix. Daniel H. Wilson's "Robopocalypse" is headed for the small screen! (Image credit: Daniel H. Wilson) Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner. "Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans. It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams. In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson. Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson: was $19 now $10.48 Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe. View Deal
summary: Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they are developing a TV adaptation of Daniel H. Wilson’s New York Times bestseller Robopocalypse. Howard will direct the pilot episode and Goldsman will serve as series showrunner, with Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment slated to executive produce.

title: Robert Pattinson auditions for James Bond, adding intrigue to casting race
content:
Sian Cain reports that Hollywood actor Robert Pattinson has auditioned for the next James Bond, joining a growing list of contenders for the iconic role.  The casting shortlist now includes Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult, according to multiple sources that confirmed the names to the Hollywood trade.

summary: Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as one of the latest contenders auditioning for the next James Bond role. The reported lineup now includes Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, Nicholas Hoult and Pattinson, according to multiple sources to Hollywood trades.

title: Look at Me by Dustin Hoffman review – an era-defining actor says his piece
content: At 89, the star of the Graduate and Rain Man demonstrates both brilliance and a startling lack of self-awareness The choice of title for an actor’s autobiography can be revealing. Sylvester Stallone went with The Steps, conflating life’s challenging progress with those steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art that Rocky euphorically ran up. Michael Douglas cheerfully and unreflectively called his One Helluva Ride. Dustin Hoffman’s is one of those that harks back to the poignantly vulnerable youthful world in which the acting bug first took effect. Al Pacino called his Sonny Boy ; Anthony Hopkins gave us We Did OK, Kid. Hoffman’s Look at Me is about the yearning to be seen and heard. Or is it about a childish impulse to show off?
summary: Look at Me by Dustin Hoffman review – an era-defining actor says his piece.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Jorge Drexler: From Uruguayan doctor to Oscar-winning singer
content:
Uruguayan singer and former doctor Jorge Drexler is set to perform at a music industry event in the basement of Madrid’s Movistar arena, where he will showcase tracks from his latest album, Taracá. The album has received eight nominations for the upcoming Latin Grammy awards, scheduled for 12 November. Drexler’s performance opens with “Guitar y Vos” (Guitar and You), a song that begins with the lines, “Long live science! Long live poetry!” He follows this with “El Otro Lado del Rio” (The Other Side of the River), which he composed for the film The Motorcycle Diaries.

Drexler gained international recognition when “El Otro Lado del Rio” won the Academy Award for best original song in 2005. At the time of the ceremony, he was largely unknown and was not invited to perform. Instead, he delivered a short a cappella version of the song in place of an acceptance speech. He continues to perform the track in this solo style, singing under a spotlight on the stairs before joining his band on stage.

His musical style incorporates the Afro-Uruguayan candombe rhythm, provided by three drummers during his live performances. One of the nominated tracks from Taracá is “Ante la Duda, Baila” (When in Doubt, Dance). The lyrics of this song reference Spanish kings and colonial governments that have historically banned various forms of dancing. Drexler’s career trajectory highlights his transition from a medical professional who grew up under an anti-music dictatorship to an Oscar-winning artist who embraces dance as a central element of his performance.
summary: Jorge Drexler, a Uruguayan doctor who began dancing at age 45, won the best original song Oscar in 2005 for his work on The Motorcycle Diaries. He is set to perform at a Madrid event ahead of the Latin Grammy awards, where his latest album Taracá has received eight nominations.

title: U2's Carnaval de Luz review: rousing, restorative rock as the band readies to take on the world
content:
U2 has released Carnaval de Luz, their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, via Island Records. The release marks a significant return for the band, which the review describes as "rousing, restorative rock" from a group ready to take on the world again.

The article notes that U2 has experienced creative turbulence over the last twenty years, struggling to match the success of their earlier works, such as Boy, Achtung Baby, and Zooropa. Previous attempts to regain relevance, including pop-oriented shifts, experimental approaches, and the 2023 rework Songs of Surrender, are described as falling short.

According to the review, the new album successfully revitalizes the band’s sound. The music is characterized as impassioned and rejuvenated, giving weight to Bono’s lyrics. The source suggests that Carnaval de Luz finally uncorks the creative genie, offering a sense of relevance that the band has not felt in many years.
summary: U2's Carnaval de Luz review: rousing, restorative rock as the band readies to take on the world.

title: Writer calls Gone Girl a feelgood movie due to dark catharsis
content:
As part of an ongoing series featuring writers discussing their preferred comfort films, a contributor identifies David Fincher’s 2014 thriller Gone Girl as a personal favorite. The writer notes that while the film’s opening narration, delivered by Ben Affleck, describes a dark and violent internal monologue, it serves as an entry point for a unique form of enjoyment. The article highlights the contrast between the film’s reputation as a devilish thriller and its function as a source of comfort for the author.

The narrative centers on Nick and Amy Dunne, portrayed by Affleck and Rosamund Pike, whose marriage deteriorates into a cycle of resentment and infidelity before Amy vanishes under suspicious circumstances. The writer explains that they are drawn to the film annually as the days shorten, finding a strange catharsis in the storyline. This comfort is derived specifically from watching the character of Amy, described as a scorned woman, execute a meticulously planned revenge, which provides a sense of dark joy despite the disturbing nature of the plot.
summary: A writer highlights David Fincher's 2014 thriller Gone Girl as a personal comfort film watched annually when days shorten. The author finds strange catharsis in watching the character Amy Dunne execute a meticulously planned revenge.
author: Guardian Culture

title: John Oliver criticizes Pete Hegseth’s military plans as ‘Dr Seuss for concussed bigots’
content: Late-night host discussed the defense secretary’s attacks on DEI, time as a Fox News host and ties to nationalist groups On his HBO show on Sunday night, John Oliver focused on Pete Hegseth, characterizing his actions as secretary of war as “taking a wrecking ball” to the US military. Oliver described Hegseth as “the guy you constantly see trying to show off by publicly exercising with troops and recruits, and to go by fitness experts on the internet, not doing a great job of it”.
summary: John Oliver addressed Pete Hegseth on his HBO show on Sunday night, denouncing Hegseth’s military plans. Oliver said Hegseth’s actions as secretary of war are “taking a wrecking ball” to the US military and mocked his habit of publicly exercising with troops and citing fitness experts.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi and Triple Purple Heart Marine, Dies at 92
content:
Donnie Dunagan, the original voice of Bambi in the Walt Disney classic, has died at the age of 92. He was also known for playing the son of Frankenstein alongside Basil Rathbone and Boris Karloff. Additionally, Dunagan served as a triple Purple Heart marine.

Dunagan was six years old when he was selected to voice the young deer in the animation’s most heartbreaking chapter. He described the recording session as easy and relaxed, utilizing rudimentary technology. An assistant director instructed him to pretend his own mother had died while voicing Bambi’s reaction to his mother being killed by a hunter.
summary: Donnie Dunagan, the original voice of Disney’s Bambi and a triple Purple Heart marine, died at age 92. He was six when he voiced the young deer and also portrayed Frankenstein’s son opposite Basil Rathbone and Boris Karloff.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Felix Nmecha’s goal sparks debate for Borussia Dortmund
content:
Felix Nmecha’s recent performances have reignited a debate surrounding his faith at Borussia Dortmund. The midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued the team during a match against Elversberg, a promoted side that had kept the home team at bay for much of the game. Nmecha’s goals proved crucial for BVB, which had been struggling with a lack of prolific scoring despite an unbeaten start to the season.

Sporting director Ole Book noted that fatigue was visible in the team, particularly after a week that included a match against Bayern Munich and a Champions League victory over Betis. Book stated that the team was too focused on managing the game. At the time of the match, Dortmund was level on points with Bayern Munich at the top of the league, though Bayern held the lead due to superior goal difference. The absence of injured center-forward Serhou Guirassy further complicated Dortmund’s offensive efforts against Elversberg.
summary: Felix Nmecha scored spectacular strikes that rescued a frustrating day for Borussia Dortmund. The celebrations after the match reignited a debate that has followed him through his career.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Shaw scores record‑extending ninth WSL hat‑trick
content:
Khadija “Bunny” Shaw extended her record by scoring a ninth WSL hat‑trick, the most in the competition’s history.  The Jamaica striker delivered a “perfect hat‑trick” for the fourth time in the league, a feat no other player has matched more than once.  In the match against West Ham, Shaw opened the scoring with a left‑foot shot, headed a second goal off the underside of the crossbar, and finished the trio with a right‑foot finish late in the game.  

Her goals helped Arsenal secure a 5‑0 victory, widening the gap at the top of the table to two points.  Shaw’s tally now places her five goals ahead of nearest rival Océane Hurtré in the race for the Golden Boot.  With the current form, it appears difficult for anyone to halt her pursuit of another top‑scoring title.
summary: Khadija “Bunny” Shaw scored a record‑extending ninth WSL hat‑trick, a perfect hat‑trick for the fourth time. The 5‑0 win over West Ham pushed her top‑scorer lead to five goals.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Manchester City to reassess after three straight defeats despite possession advantage
content: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics Sign up for our free newsletter here Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here.
summary: Enzo Maresca says Manchester City will reassess after three straight defeats despite having more possession and chances in each loss. The losses are unusual, as City had higher possession and more chances in all three games.
author: Guardian Sport

title: New Gambling Policy Commission to Review UK Betting Laws, Chaired by Jagjit Chadha OBE
content:
A review of the 2005 Gambling Act has been described as “analogue” in a digital age, and a new commission will examine whether the current legal framework requires reform. The commission, called the Gambling Policy Commission (GPC), will be staffed by experts in economics, law, public policy, health and sport. It will conduct an independent, evidence‑based assessment of the existing gambling framework and consider whether new primary legislation might be necessary.

The GPC is chaired by Jagjit Chadha OBE, a professor of economics at Cambridge University. It will launch on Monday and immediately issue a call for evidence from all interested parties and individuals. Submissions must be received by 12 February 2027. The commission aims to deliver its findings and recommendations before the next general election, with the outcome expected to shape the future funding model for racing and other betting‑dependent activities.
summary: The Gambling Policy Commission, chaired by Jagjit Chadha OBE, will launch on Monday and call for evidence from all interested parties until 12 February 2027. It aims to deliver findings and recommendations before the next general election, reviewing the existing gambling framework to assess the need for further reform.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England’s back three faces injuries after rout of Australia, Borthwick warned
content:
England’s emphatic win over the Wallabies on Sunday marked the first time in two years that head coach Scott Borthwick fielded his preferred back‑three of Immanuel Feyi‑Waboso, Tommy Freeman and George Furbank. It was also the first occasion the trio lined up wearing the numbers 11, 14 and 15 on their respective backs.

Feyi‑Waboso sustained an ankle injury that will rule him out for the remainder of the autumn campaign. George Furbank is dealing with a groin problem that will keep him sidelined against Japan, and Borthwick is considering resting some players, which could mean Freeman sits out on Saturday. As a result, the side may feature an entirely different back‑three against Eddie Jones’s Australia.
summary: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Tommy Freeman and George Furbank can make an impact at next year’s World Cup, providing they can all stay fit Rugby, at its heart, is a simple game. Win the collisions and you’ll more than likely win the match.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Manchester United Weighs Sacking of Michael Carrick as Wilcox Leads Review
content:
Manchester United are weighing the possibility of sacking head coach Michael Carrick.  Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, is leading a review after Carrick was given the Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa matches to turn results around.  Wilcox is consulting with Omar Berrada, the chief executive, before making a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy.  

United are currently in the Premier League relegation zone and have recorded only three victories in 15 games across all competitions.  Carrick was given time after defeats to Como and Bournemouth, but the club’s performance has prompted the review.
summary: Manchester United is reviewing the potential sacking of Michael Carrick, with director of football Jason Wilcox leading the assessment. The review will involve consultation with chief executive Omar Berrada and a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, as United sit in the Premier League relegation zone with only three wins in 15 games.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Rob Hawkins Overcomes Illness to Become Key Player for England Rugby League
content: Rob Hawkins replied to an advert he believed advertised wheelchair basketball in 2014. He later became a key member of England’s squad defending their Rugby League World Cup title.
summary: Rob Hawkins replied to an advert for wheelchair basketball in 2014, unaware it would lead to a spot on England's Rugby League squad defending their World Cup title. He overcame illness to become a key player for the side.
author: BBC Sport

title: Ben White says England selection exile story remains unknown
content: Arsenal defender Ben White said people do not know the full story behind his decision to make himself unavailable for England selection. He added that he would make the same decision again.
summary: Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the full story behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection. He added that he would make the same decision again.
author: BBC Sport

title: Man Utd board yet to decide Michael Carrick's future after worst start in 40 years
content:
Manchester United’s board have not yet decided on Michael Carrick’s future.  
This uncertainty comes amid the club’s worst start to a campaign in 40 years.
summary: Manchester United's board have not made a final decision on Michael Carrick's future. This uncertainty persists despite the club recording its worst start to a campaign in 40 years.
author: BBC Sport

title: Vance jokes about 'devastating loss' at veterans event
content: Vice President Mike Vance joked about a “devastating loss” during a veterans’ event in Washington on Monday. He clarified that the remark referred to football, not the GOP’s midterm election results. Vance began his address by noting he wanted to talk about the loss before moving on to his main remarks.
summary: Vice President Vance joked about a "devastating loss" while addressing veterans in Washington on Monday. The remark, which appeared to reference GOP midterm election losses, was actually about football.
author: The Hill

title: Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff despite midterm losses
content: President Trump’s recent appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff signals a continued hard‑line stance. After the Republican losses in the midterms, many expected the president to reassess his strategy. Instead, Trump appears to be doubling down on his current approach.
summary: President Trump selected Stephen Miller as chief of staff following midterm elections where Republicans faced significant losses. The article suggests this decision indicates a strategy to double down rather than reassess.
author: The Hill

title: 150+ immigration groups urge Democrats to cut enforcement funding and create citizenship pathways
content: A coalition of over 150 immigration rights organizations and allies has urged Democrats to prioritize immigration policy upon taking control of the next Congress. In a letter sent Monday and first shared with Politico, the groups called for cutting funding to federal immigration enforcement agencies and establishing a pathway to citizenship.
summary: A coalition of more than 150 immigration rights organizations and allies urged Democrats to cut funding for federal immigration enforcement agencies and create a citizenship pathway if the party takes control of the next Congress. The groups sent a letter on Monday, first shared with Politico.
author: The Hill

title: Massie reads impeachment articles against Hegseth as Congress returns to DC
content: Massie read articles of impeachment against Hegseth as Congress returned to Washington. The session follows a week‑long break and a dramatic shift in the midterm election that left Republicans at a disadvantage. Senate Republicans blame President Trump for the loss of both chambers and face a large to‑do list, including government funding.
summary: Massie reads articles of impeachment against Hegseth as Congress returns to Washington. Senate Republicans are furious with President Trump, blaming him for the loss of both chambers and facing a massive to-do list, including funding the government.
author: The Hill

title: Jeffries speaks to reporters after Congress returns for lame‑duck session
content: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D‑N. Y.) will speak to reporters Monday afternoon after Congress returned to Washington following Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories. He is poised to become Speaker when Democrats take control of the House in January and faces several challenges as his party prepares to transition into the majority.
summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N. Y.) will speak to reporters Monday afternoon after Congress returned to Washington following Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories.
author: The Hill

title: Murkowski to seek GOP ranking on Senate Appropriations Committee
content: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) plans to seek the ranking member position on the Senate Appropriations Committee, her office confirmed to The Hill. This move follows the reelection loss of current Chair Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) last week. Murkowski, described as a moderate Republican who often bucks her party, will need to work with colleagues to lead the GOP on the powerful committee.
summary: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) plans to lead Republicans on the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.
author: The Hill

title: Massie to speak Monday in push for Hegseth impeachment vote
content: Rep. Thomas Massie (R‑Ky.) is scheduled to speak on Monday as he pushes for a House vote to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Massie has introduced eight articles of impeachment, alleging that Hegseth violated congressional war powers, suppressed free speech, and authorized unlawful military operations, including in Iran and Venezuela.
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is set to speak Monday as he pushes to force a House vote on ousting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
author: The Hill

title: Sen. Chris Coons Calls for Probe into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Alleged Affair with Chinese Spy
content: Senator Chris Coons (D‑Del.) announced on Monday that he is seeking an investigation into reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Coons, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he is pushing to examine whether Nvidia’s operations could have compromised U.S. national security. He posted the call on the social‑media platform X.
summary: Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) on Monday called for a probe into reporting that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
author: The Hill

title: Midterm results could complicate JD Vance's future after serving as Trump's No.2
content: Midterm results could complicate JD Vance’s political future. Vice President JD Vance is looking to recast his political fortune after serving as the Trump administration’s No. 2 while his party suffered a historic wipeout.
summary: Vice President JD Vance is looking to recast his political fortune after serving as the Trump administration's No. 2. His party suffered a historic wipeout in the midterm elections.
author: NPR Politics

title: Palantir hires former Senator Jon Tester amid new Congress scrutiny
content: Palantir has hired former Democratic Senator Jon Tester as it faces scrutiny in the new Congress. The company has been accused of allowing its powerful software tools to be used by the Trump administration to surveil Americans. Hiring Tester is seen as an effort to burnish its image.
summary: Palantir has been accused of letting its powerful tools be used by the Trump administration to surveil Americans. Now it is hiring former Sen. Jon Tester to burnish its image.
author: NPR Politics

title: Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect
content: Lawmakers return to Washington this week following the midterm elections. Republicans intend to complete work on several pending issues before Democrats assume control of Congress in January.
summary: Lawmakers are coming back to Washington this week after the midterm elections. Republicans plan to finish work on several outstanding issues before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
author: NPR Politics

title: Supreme Court weighs case on suing federal officers for injuries
content: The Supreme Court is weighing a case involving a prisoner who suffered severe injuries and was subsequently denied medical care while incarcerated. The individual seeks to sue a prison nurse, a legal action that could alter the standards for holding federal officers accountable. This review occurs as the Court considers efforts to shield federal law enforcement agencies, a matter gaining attention amid rising complaints against ICE.
summary: The Supreme Court is considering a case involving a prisoner who suffered brutal injuries and was denied medical care. The prisoner seeks to sue a prison nurse in a case that could change laws on holding federal officers accountable.
author: NPR Politics

title: Democrats won big in midterms, voters hope for grocery bill relief.
content: Affordability concerns dominated voter priorities during the midterms, driven by rising prices for food and other goods due to tariffs and the war in Iran. With Democrats securing a significant victory, Americans now anticipate that Washington will provide relief from these escalating costs.
summary: Affordability concerns were top of mind for voters heading into the midterms, as tariffs and the war in Iran drove up prices, including food costs. Americans are now expecting relief from Washington.
author: NPR Politics

title: Trump Appoints Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff; GOP Holds Congress
content: Republicans have only weeks remaining before losing control of Congress, prompting an overview of anticipated developments. Additionally, Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, a move that signals his readiness to confront his opposition.
summary: Republicans have only weeks left to control Congress. Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, signaling readiness to confront opposition.
author: NPR Politics

title: Elle Hunt: Marine park whales teach us to value other species
content:
Elle Hunt, a freelance journalist, argues that the current state of marine ecosystems necessitates a move beyond simplistic environmental slogans like “Save the whales.” While this campaign helped secure the 1986 global ban on commercial whaling, Hunt contends that the phrase now appears reductive and naive. She notes that Greenpeace recently emphasized on its website that significant work remains to protect whales four decades after that ban.

Hunt maintains that humans must recognize their actions are not easily undone, particularly regarding the trauma inflicted on mammals in facilities such as Marineland in Canada. She asserts that there is no way to “save” these animals from such environments, suggesting that the grim reality of their situation could lead to a positive outcome only if it teaches society to value other species.
summary: Elle Hunt argues that there is no way to save traumatised mammals from places like Marineland in Canada. She states that humans need to understand that their actions are not easily undone.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Fog traps emissions, raising England’s urban air pollution to very high
content:
On Monday, air pollution in England’s urban areas reached very high levels, according to government monitoring. Still, foggy conditions trapped emissions after a weekend of fireworks and bonfires, which likely contributed to concentrations well above the WHO daily guideline for particulate matter.

Monitoring data showed 11 sites—primarily in London and Greater Manchester—recorded the highest band on the 10‑point index for particulate matter in the 24‑hour period ending at 10 a.m. A further 27 sites across the capital, the north‑west, the Midlands, Yorkshire, and the east of England reported high levels.
summary: Government monitoring showed 11 sites, mainly in London and Greater Manchester, reached the highest band on its 10‑point index for particulate matter in the 24 hours to 10am. A further 27 sites recorded "high" levels across the capital, the north‑west, the Midlands, Yorkshire and the east of England.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Senate votes on bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy
content:
A 417‑page bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), is set for an initial procedural Senate vote on Monday. The legislation would streamline the approval of large infrastructure projects across the United States, including fossil‑fuel pipelines and transmission lines that would expand clean‑energy capacity on the grid. In exchange for faster construction, the bill would roll back environmental and social protections that currently apply to such projects.

The act is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate. Former President Donald Trump has urged all senators to support the measure. However, following last week’s “blue wave” elections, several environmental and tribal advocates have asked Democratic leaders to pause the vote, reflecting a split among climate advocates over the bill’s impact on environmental safeguards.
summary: Senate votes on bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Seasonal allergies can trigger sinus symptoms and raise risk of bacterial sinusitis
content: Frequent sinus symptoms that appear with the seasons are often linked to allergies. Seasonal allergies can produce congestion, drainage, facial pressure and fatigue. The inflammation from these allergies can also raise the likelihood of bacterial sinusitis, a common type of sinus infection.
summary: Seasonal allergies can cause congestion, drainage, facial pressure and fatigue. The inflammation from allergies can increase the risk of bacterial sinusitis.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Fear of Falling Triggers Activity Avoidance and Heightens Fall Risk
content: Fear of falling can lead people to avoid stairs, exercise, and other daily activities. Paradoxically, that same fear may heighten the risk of a fall. The article highlights how common concerns about falling can both restrict routine movements and increase actual fall risk.
summary: A fear of falling may cause people to avoid stairs, exercise and other daily activities. But that fear can also increase the risk of a fall.
author: Medical Xpress

title: COVID-19 tracing apps had limited impact as governments failed to integrate them, review finds
content: A comparative review published in the International Journal of Services, Economics and Management found that digital contact‑tracing apps had only a limited effect on COVID‑19 transmission. The paper notes that while public apathy was cited as a factor, the primary issue was that governments and public health authorities did not integrate the technology effectively into their pandemic response. The authors suggest that this lesson should be heeded before the next pandemic.
summary: COVID-19 tracing apps had limited impact as governments failed to integrate them, review finds.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Karolinska Institutet finds two new amyloid‑beta forms in Alzheimer's
content:
Researchers at Karolinska Institutet and collaborators identified two previously unknown forms of amyloid‑beta that may contribute to Alzheimer’s. The study, published in Nature Communications, highlights these forms as potential disease drivers.  

The same study shows that a protein previously discovered by the researchers can counteract the formation of these harmful amyloid‑beta forms, pointing to a possible new treatment approach.
summary: Researchers at Karolinska Institutet and collaborators identified two previously unknown amyloid‑beta forms that may contribute to Alzheimer's development. The Nature Communications study also shows a protein the researchers previously discovered can counteract formation of these harmful forms, suggesting a potential new treatment approach.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Computer Simulations Suggest Pre-Chemotherapy Hematopoietic Support Improves Leukemia Treatment
content:
Researchers at Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg used computer simulations to evaluate 323 treatment protocols for a specific leukemia therapy. The study found that a drug used to support blood‑cell production (hematopoiesis) may be more effective when given before chemotherapy rather than after it.

The work was led by mathematicians Professor Dr. Sebastian Sager, Dr. Adrian Reimann and Anna Gebhard of the Institute of Mathematical Optimization. Their findings suggest a potential adjustment to treatment timing that could improve outcomes in leukemia care.
summary: A drug used to support blood cell production (hematopoiesis) could be more effective in a specific leukemia treatment if administered before chemotherapy rather than after it. This was the outcome of computer simulations that involved researchers from Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Watching sports associated with fewer depressive symptoms in adults with congenital heart disease
content:
Researchers at the University of Tsukuba found that watching sports more frequently is associated with fewer depressive symptoms in adults with congenital heart disease (CHD). Specifically, attending sporting events in person at least once in the previous year and watching sports on television or the internet at least once a week were each linked to reduced depressive symptoms.

These findings suggest that watching sports may serve as an accessible leisure activity contributing to the mental well-being of adults with CHD. The study’s results have been published in the European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing.
summary: Watching sports associated with fewer depressive symptoms in adults with congenital heart disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Lund University study shows reprogrammed cancer cells recruit immune cells in tumors
content:
A new international study led by Lund University in Sweden has shown that reprogrammed cancer cells can help orchestrate the immune system’s attack on tumors.  

In experiments with mice, researchers observed how immune cells are recruited and organized within tumors to mount an immune response.  

The findings could pave the way for more effective immunotherapy and, ultimately, help more patients benefit from the treatment.
summary: Researchers from Lund University in Sweden conducted a study showing that reprogrammed cancer cells can orchestrate the immune system's attack on tumors. Experiments in mice demonstrated that immune cells are recruited and organized within tumors, potentially leading to more effective immunotherapy.
author: Medical Xpress

title: North Carolina CPR and EMS program fails to boost cardiac arrest survival
content: A comprehensive emergency‑medical‑services and community‑based educational program in North Carolina aimed at improving recognition of out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest and encouraging bystander CPR and automated external defibrillator use was evaluated. The preliminary, independent analysis presented on Sunday at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions in Chicago found that the intervention did not significantly increase patient survival with favorable brain function. The findings were reported as late‑breaking science at the conference.
summary: A comprehensive EMS and community‑based educational intervention in North Carolina targeted out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest recognition and increased bystander CPR and AED use. The program did not significantly improve patient survival with favorable brain function, according to new independent preliminary data presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions in Chicago.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Eli Lilly’s Foundayo pill eases sleep apnea in late-stage trial, paving way for approval
content: Eli Lilly’s obesity pill, Foundayo, showed a reduction in sleep apnea symptoms in a late‑stage trial. The company plans to file for U.S. approval by the end of the year for the daily pill, targeting adults with obesity who have moderate‑to‑severe obstructive sleep apnea.
summary: Lilly plans to file by the end of the year for U. S.
author: CNBC Business

title: Boeing to cut about 5% of its commercial plane workforce
content:
Boeing announced on Monday that it will reduce its commercial plane workforce by approximately 5% as it slows the pace of increasing jet production. The company stated it will eliminate these positions through a combination of layoffs and natural attrition.

Stephanie Pope, Boeing’s commercial chief, explained in a message to employees that the slower ramp-up is intended to provide factories and supply chain partners with additional time to achieve stability.
summary: Boeing announced it will cut about 5% of its commercial plane workforce through layoffs and attrition. The cuts are intended to slow the ramp‑up of jet production and give factories and supply chain partners more time to achieve stability, according to a message from commercial chief Stephanie Pope.
author: Guardian Business

title: Democrats promise economic relief after massive midterm win
content:
Senator Chuck Schumer announced at a press conference last week that “relief is on the way” for cash‑strapped Americans, celebrating the Democrats’ massive midterm victory. In the remarks, he highlighted the party’s pledge to cut costs and improve the economy.

The winning candidates also promised to lower food and healthcare expenses, rein in corporations that they say are ripping off consumers and workers, curb billionaire power, and make the world’s biggest economy better serve the working class.
summary: Senator Chuck Schumer said relief is on the way in a press conference after Democrats’ massive midterms win. Winning candidates pledged to cut food and healthcare costs, rein in corporations, curb billionaire power and improve the economy.
author: Guardian Business

title: Nvidia’s value tumbles by $330bn after ‘honeytrap’ investigation launched, as China denies spying claims – business live
content: Shares in world’s most valuable company hit seven-month low after CEO Huang admits to affair, after allegations of relationship with Chinese spy Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence Huang is receiving support from some fellow tech executives, including Elon Musk. Musk commented “I agree” on a post by ​Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang “did something incredibly dumb” that was “bad for America” but that “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”. “While Nvidia has sought to reassure us all, ​there are several layers here, beginning with the unfortunate timing. “For example: The company is systemically important for tech, markets and the economy; Investors tend to struggle to price in key-person and governance issues; and there are fluid national security and geopolitical dynamics.”
summary: Nvidia’s value tumbles by $330bn after ‘honeytrap’ investigation launched, as China denies spying claims – business live.
author: Guardian Business

title: High-pressure setup unlocks measurements of organized structures in turbulent flows
content:
Turbulent flows are found in clouds, the ocean, and other planets. Despite their chaotic nature, they form large‑scale structures that can be calculated and predicted.  

For instance, long streaks of clouds may look orderly from the outside, yet their interiors are intensely turbulent.
summary: Turbulent flows are found in clouds, oceans, and other planets, and they form large-scale structures that can be calculated and predicted. Long streaks of clouds appear orderly from the outside, but their interiors are characterized by intense turbulence.
author: Phys.org

title: Pollutants threaten rivers and streams even in protected areas
content:
A new study from RPTU University Kaiserslautern‑Landau has shown that organic pollutants—such as pesticides and industrial chemicals—continue to pose risks to aquatic ecosystems, even in protected rivers and streams. The research drew on more than 180 million water measurements collected through France’s long‑term monitoring program “Naïades.”

The analysis found pollutants detectable in nearly all of the water bodies examined. It also highlighted that groups of substances that had been overlooked in earlier studies now appear to contribute significantly to environmental risks.
summary: Pollutants threaten rivers and streams even in protected areas.
author: Phys.org

title: Kari Schleher's Study Traces Azurite Sources for Ancestral Pueblo
content: Kari Schleher, an assistant professor in the University of New Mexico’s Department of Anthropology and faculty curator of archaeology at UNM’s Maxwell Museum, has published research on azurite, a vivid blue copper mineral. Her study explores whether archaeologists can trace the mineral’s ancient Pueblo sources, noting its use by the Ancestral Pueblo people for at least 1,400 years.
summary: Kari Schleher, assistant professor in the University of New Mexico's Department of Anthropology and faculty curator of archaeology at UNM's Maxwell Museum, published research on azurite sources. The study investigates whether archaeologists can determine the origins of azurite, a vivid blue copper mineral used by the Ancestral Pueblo people at least 1,400 years ago.
author: Phys.org

title: Southern Ocean identified as key factor in Earth's warmest climate in 65 million years
content: About 50 million years ago, Earth’s climate reached its warmest point since the dinosaurs died out. Global temperatures were more than 10 °C above today’s averages, and atmospheric CO₂ concentrations climbed to roughly 1,600 parts per million. Scientists have long wondered how such high CO₂ levels were maintained for millions of years. An international research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry has identified the Southern Ocean as a key factor in sustaining that elevated greenhouse‑gas concentration.
summary: About 50 million years ago, Earth experienced its warmest climate since the extinction of the dinosaurs. Global temperatures were more than 10°C higher than today, and atmospheric CO₂ concentrations reached around 1,600 parts per million.
author: Phys.org

title: Long-lived mineral grains key to reconstructing planetary impact events
content:
Long‑lived mineral grains can be invaluable for reconstructing impact events, but the stories are complex.  

Reconstructing impact events on Earth and other planetary bodies, including the moon, is crucial for understanding how the solar system evolved and how planets develop.
summary: Long-lived mineral grains can be invaluable for reconstructing impact events, but their stories are complex. Reconstructing impact events on Earth, the moon, and other planetary bodies helps understand solar system evolution and planet development.
author: Phys.org

title: CSIRO scientist uses instruments to detect hidden wheat weaknesses
content: Aswin Singaram Natarajan, a senior experimental scientist at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, notes that human eyes can be deceived by wheat plants that appear healthy. He explains that a plant might look green and vital while still suffering from significant issues, such as losing too much energy or water, or filling its grain to ripeness too slowly. These specific weaknesses are invisible to the human eye but are clearly detectable with the appropriate scientific instruments.
summary: Aswin Singaram Natarajan, a senior experimental scientist at CSIRO, notes that wheat plants can appear healthy while suffering from invisible issues. These weaknesses, such as excessive energy or water loss, are detectable by instruments but not by the human eye.
author: Phys.org

title: Atomic Defects Leave Distinct Optical Fingerprints in Quantum Materials
content: Atomic defects in quantum materials, though essential for future technologies, are hard to detect. They change the material’s light‑response, creating a distinct optical fingerprint that scientists can measure. The main difficulty lies in determining which fingerprint corresponds to which specific defect.
summary: Tiny atomic defects in quantum materials alter how the material responds to light, producing a distinctive optical fingerprint that scientists can measure. The challenge is figuring out which fingerprints belong to which defects.
author: Phys.org

title: Ultracold Potassium Atoms Reveal First Ultraquantum Turbulence
content: An experiment with ultracold potassium atoms has revealed details of a type of turbulence that only exists in the quantum realm and relies on odd tangles of stringy whirlpools
summary: An experiment with ultracold potassium atoms revealed details of a turbulence type that only exists in the quantum realm. The turbulence relies on odd tangles of stringy whirlpools.
author: New Scientist

title: Schrödinger’s cat paradox explained by missing time physics
content: A new approach proposes that certain bizarre effects in quantum theory may result from physics failing to adequately account for time. This perspective offers an alternative explanation for phenomena often described as inexplicable within the standard framework.
summary: A radical new approach suggests some of quantum theory’s most bizarre and inexplicable effects might be down to physics failing to account properly for time. The approach applies to the Schrödinger’s cat scenario, suggesting the paradox arises from time treatment.
author: New Scientist

title: X Chromosome Gene ZFX May Lower Autism Rates in Women and Girls
content: A gene named ZFX significantly influences a network of genes associated with autism, potentially explaining why the condition is less prevalent in females.
summary: The gene ZFX influences a network of autism‑related genes. This may explain the lower prevalence of autism in females.
author: New Scientist

title: Columnist Michael Marshall says ancient humans ate many insects
content: Columnist Michael Marshall reports that ancient humans may have consumed significantly more insects than previously believed. While discussions of prehistoric diets typically center on meat or cereal grains, Marshall’s research suggests that insects played a larger role in the meals of early people.
summary: Columnist Michael Marshall argues that prehistoric diets included more insects. He suggests ancient humans may have eaten insects more than previously thought.
author: New Scientist

title: Study shows cold therapy may hinder post-exercise recovery
content: Many are convinced that ice baths or cold showers are an effective way to speed recovery after exercise, but a study finds that cold therapy may actually have the opposite effect
summary: A study found that cold therapy, such as ice baths or cold showers, may worsen recovery after exercise. The findings suggest that doing nothing might be better than using cold therapy.
author: New Scientist

title: Gut bacteria may eat intestinal mucus when fiber intake is low
content: Scientists have found that gut bacteria consume the protective mucus lining of intestines when fiber is scarce, producing potentially harmful compounds. Fiber helps prevent this activity, while overlooked proteins in plant foods shift bacteria toward producing beneficial substances. These findings offer a new explanation for the health benefits of plant-based diets.
summary: Scientists found that gut bacteria feed on the protective mucus lining of the intestines and produce potentially harmful compounds when fiber is absent. Proteins in plant foods help shift these bacteria toward producing beneficial substances.
author: Science Daily

title: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
content: Scientists have observed a quantum state of matter at room temperature that exhibits the structure of a crystal alongside the frictionless flow of a liquid. This breakthrough removes a significant practical limitation associated with exotic quantum experiments. The development may accelerate the realization of advanced light-based computing and sensing technologies.
summary: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists Find Acorn Production Predicts Lyme Disease Tick Surges Two Years Ahead
content:
Scientists have identified new factors influencing Lyme disease risk after more than 35 years of research. Contrary to previous assumptions, deer populations appear less significant than mice, which can cause a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Additionally, acorn production serves as a predictor for tick population surges two years in advance.

The study also suggests that extreme temperatures may be less lethal to ticks than previously believed. These findings highlight the critical role of small mammals and environmental conditions in driving tick populations, offering a different perspective on the drivers of Lyme disease risk.
summary: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have discovered that mice, not deer, are the main drivers of Lyme disease risk. The study also shows that acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance and that extreme temperatures may be less deadly to ticks than previously thought.
author: Science Daily

title: DNA analysis of Shroud of Turin uncovers complex biological traces
content: DNA analysis of the Shroud of Turin has revealed a complex mixture of biological traces, offering new insights into the artifact’s history. These scientific findings provide a fresh perspective on the centuries-old mystery, highlighting the various environments the cloth encountered over time.
summary: Scientists performed DNA analysis on the Shroud of Turin and found a complex mixture of biological traces. These traces could provide new insights into the cloth's history and the environments it has encountered.
author: Science Daily

title: Osteoporosis Drugs May Cut Dementia Risk by 24% in Study of 120,000 Older Adults
content: A new study involving over 120,000 older adults indicates that common osteoporosis drugs may lower the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. These findings suggest that medications currently used to strengthen bones could potentially offer protective benefits for the aging brain.
summary: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults found that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The findings suggest that medications used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.
author: Science Daily

title: Caltech robot builds part of space structure for first time
content:
For the first time, a robot has autonomously built part of a structure in space, marking a breakthrough that could fundamentally change space exploration.  

The technology may eventually enable scientists to construct enormous telescopes, communications antennas, and solar power stations in orbit, surpassing the size limits of today’s rockets.
summary: A Caltech robot autonomously built part of a structure in space for the first time. This breakthrough could enable scientists to construct enormous telescopes, communications antennas, and solar power stations in orbit, beyond the size limits of today's rockets.

title: NASA reveals accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028
content:
NASA announced an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028. SpaceX and Blue Origin are developing competing lunar landers, and a crucial orbital test is scheduled for 2027.  

Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.
summary: NASA has announced an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and an orbital test slated for 2027. The plan includes faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions to support a permanent lunar presence and future Mars exploration.

title: Scientists find pantethine supplement may help fight psoriasis
content:
Scientists discovered that pantethine, a vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis.  

In animal studies, the supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and, in a small human trial, showed promising results, revealing an unexpected link between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.
summary: Researchers reported that pantethine, a vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, suggesting a link between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

content: The author shared the solution to a recent puzzle from the International Maths Kangaroo, a multiple-choice challenge taken by over seven million children annually. The post includes the original problem and its answer, referencing a previous story about the event.

title: Doctors report breakthrough trial for stiff person syndrome, enabling patients to work
content: Doctors say a new trial has produced a potentially significant breakthrough in treating stiff‑person syndrome (SPS), the rare autoimmune condition that also affects singer Céline Dion. The experimental therapy enabled some participants to return to work and resume hobbies, marking the first reported functional improvements in the disease. SPS attacks the central nervous system, causing severe rigidity and painful muscle spasms, and, according to the report, no cure has been found despite decades of research.
summary: Doctors have reported a potentially significant breakthrough in treating stiff person syndrome, the autoimmune condition that affects singer Céline Dion. In the trial, some patients have been able to return to work and resume hobbies, though no cure currently exists.
author: Guardian Science

title: CHAPEA Mission 2 Crew Reflects After 378 Days on Simulated Mars
content:
The CHAPEA (Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog) Mission 2 crew completed a year‑long Mars surface simulation on October 31, 2026, when the four volunteers stepped out of NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. The 378‑day mission began on October 19, 2025, and the crew—Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer, and Matthew Montgomery—worked in a roughly 1,700‑square‑foot, 3‑D‑printed habitat that lacked windows, outside sound, and real‑time communication with family and friends.

During the simulation the crew performed simulated Marswalks, operated a drone and a rover, maintained the habitat, exercised, and cultivated crops. The mission was supported by NASA researchers and ground teams who collected health and performance data while the crew navigated limited resources and a 22‑minute communication delay. The experience was framed as a preparation for future human exploration beyond Earth, with the goal of gathering knowledge to protect crew health and performance for lunar and Martian missions.

NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway compared the crew’s isolation to his own 237‑day space station mission, noting that the same period saw Artemis II astronauts travel around the Moon and set a record for the farthest distance humans have traveled from Earth. The agency also celebrated 25 years of continuous human presence aboard the International Space Station on November 2, 2025.

Each crew member brought a distinct skill set. Ross Elder, the commander and a U.S. Air Force test pilot, led simulated Marswalks and emphasized nutrition, exercise, and rest. Ellen Ellis, a U.S. Space Force officer, served as medical officer and organized biological sample collection, stressing the need for an integrated ground team. James Spicer, a flight engineer with satellite communications experience, maintained habitat systems and managed consumables, while Matthew Montgomery, a science officer with hardware engineering and indoor agriculture expertise, handled rock sample identification and hydroponic crop cultivation.

Post‑mission evaluations will last two weeks, during which researchers will interpret the crew’s data alongside their experiences. Principal investigator Grace Douglas said the study will help NASA weigh human health and performance risks against resources such as crew time, communication capacity, and life‑support system designs. Project scientist Sara Whiting noted that the data arrive at a critical time as NASA plans the first lunar outpost near the Moon’s South Pole. The CHAPEA Mission 2 crew’s completion marks a significant step in preparing for future exploration of the Moon and Mars.
summary: Four research volunteers completed a 378‑day simulated Mars mission in NASA’s 1,700‑square‑foot, 3D‑printed Mars Dune Alpha habitat, exiting on Oct. 31, 2026. They gathered health and performance data while conducting simulated Marswalks, robotic operations, habitat maintenance, exercise, and crop cultivation to inform future human exploration beyond Earth.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Astronauts of Different Eras Share Stage at Artemis Celebration Gala
content:
Purpose Entertainment hosted the Artemis Celebration Gala on November 6, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida. The event took place on the eve of NASA’s MAX POWER event and served as a signature conclusion to the nation’s 250th anniversary celebration. The gala was designed to honor explorers, innovators, and visionaries who are advancing the next era of human spaceflight.

The celebration marked the successful completion of the agency’s Artemis II mission, a milestone in America’s return to deep space exploration. While commemorating these achievements, the event also looked forward to humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the ongoing Artemis campaign.

NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Luca Parmitano, Russell “Rusty” Schweickart, Frank Rubio, and Bob Hines shared the stage during the gala. The gathering highlighted the collaborative efforts behind the agency’s recent successes and its future goals for lunar exploration.
summary: From left: NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Luca Parmitano, Russell “Rusty” Schweickart, Frank Rubio, and Bob Hines onstage at the Artemis Celebration Gala at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida, on Nov. 6, 2026.
author: NASA News

title: Rising living costs test UK's net zero ambitions
content:
In 2026, the United Kingdom experienced a series of severe weather events—including floods, wildfires, and heatwaves—that underscored the tangible impact of climate change on the country’s climate.  

The article questions whether the government’s commitment to achieving net‑zero emissions will be challenged by the rising cost of living, suggesting that economic pressures could influence future climate‑change policy decisions.
summary: The article notes that floods, wildfires, and heatwaves in 2026 have made the impact of climate change on UK weather hard to ignore. It asks whether soaring living costs will affect the government's commitment to tackling climate change.
author: BBC Science

title: Lubrizol integrates AI and cloud computing to accelerate specialty chemicals R&D
content:
Specialty chemicals maker Lubrizol is using artificial intelligence, cloud computing and advanced modeling to speed innovation while maintaining product performance. The company’s digital strategy focuses on giving researchers tools to test ideas faster, make better‑informed decisions and develop more sustainable materials, according to Girish Rao, Lubrizol’s vice president of information technology.

Rao says Lubrizol is building a digital foundation that links business processes, modern data platforms and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development teams. The approach combines decades of technical data with the expertise of chemists and engineers, allowing data scientists to identify patterns, test hypotheses and model possibilities before physical experiments are run. He emphasizes that the goal is not to replace scientific judgment but to provide better tools for scientists.

To align differing perspectives—experimental validity, model performance and platform security—the company forms “fusion teams” of scientists, data scientists and IT staff. These teams start with small pilots to build trust, after which they can create value more effectively. Cloud infrastructure gives Lubrizol flexible access to computing resources and modern tools without the need for large data‑center investments.

Lubrizol sees digital modeling as a way to evaluate more formulations, explore alternatives such as starch and corn‑based materials, and assess life‑cycle trade‑offs, supporting sustainability goals. Rao projects that AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins and connected data will converge, making laboratories smarter and manufacturing plants more efficient, provided the capabilities are integrated responsibly and at scale. This webcast was produced in partnership with Infosys and created by MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm.
summary: Lubrizol is building a digital foundation that connects cloud infrastructure and data platforms with scientific expertise to help researchers test ideas faster. The company uses "fusion teams" of scientists, data scientists, and IT staff to develop sustainable materials while balancing performance and regulatory constraints.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Nvidia Investigating CEO Jensen Huang Over Spy Affair
content:
The weekday newsletter “The Download” delivers a concise snapshot of current technology headlines. In this edition, two stories stand out: a critique of the climate‑change narrative surrounding artificial intelligence and an investigation into Nvidia’s leadership.

The opinion piece, written by Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at UCLA School of Law and former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, founder of the sustainability research firm Dual Citizen, argues that the “climate case for AI” has not yet been made. They note that as nations convene in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, the host has urged countries to commit to designing, powering, and deploying AI in ways that support climate action. However, the authors observe that industries worldwide are not yet harnessing AI to reduce greenhouse‑gas emissions. While AI companies frequently make optimistic claims about the technology’s potential to address climate change, the reality, according to Nichols and Tamanini, is less promising.

A separate feature spotlights forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich. Dent is part of an international research network that studies the complex networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some tropical forests to recover after destruction. The network’s goal is to offer a low‑cost, high‑impact alternative to traditional carbon‑crediting schemes, which often involve planting large areas with a single species of tree. Over more than a decade, Dent’s research has shown that large “monocrop” programs can be expensive mistakes and that resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, restoring ecosystems that absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide.

The newsletter’s “must‑reads” section lists a range of tech stories. Nvidia is under investigation after its CEO, Jensen Huang, admitted to an intimate relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia shares fell 5 % in pre‑market trading, and Huang’s children are also employed by the company. Democrats are reportedly planning investigations into major tech firms, beginning with Apple, Meta, and Elon Musk’s companies, in an effort to address data‑center concerns and regulate the AI sector. The United Nations’ annual climate meeting began today, marking the first conference after confirmation that the planet will exceed 1.5 °C warming. Other stories cover the risks of connecting refrigerators to the internet, Tesla’s decision to discontinue the Cybertruck, potential Iranian attacks on subsea cables, challenges faced by Chinese AI labs in recruiting Silicon Valley talent, the resurgence of online piracy, a Japanese moon‑landing plan, and a Philadelphia delivery‑robot controversy. The newsletter also includes a quote from Jensen Huang, in which he apologizes to Nvidia employees for his affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
summary: Nvidia is investigating its CEO, Jensen Huang, after he admitted to an intimate relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The investigation comes amid a 5% drop in Nvidia shares in pre‑market trading.
