title: Backlash against data centers driven by electricity demand, not culture war
content: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport. Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

title: Scientists Identify Massive Starless Galaxy Candidate with 2 Billion Masses of Hydrogen
content: Scientists have identified a promising candidate for a massive starless galaxy. The object is estimated to contain about two billion times the Sun’s mass in hydrogen while showing no detectable stars. Researchers say that examining this galaxy could address questions that have long challenged astronomers.
summary: The candidate galaxy contains roughly 2 billion times the Sun’s mass in hydrogen and appears to have no stars. Studying the object could help answer questions that have vexed astronomers for years.

title: Hulu docuseries 'Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death' probes Thai male influencers' deaths
content: Hulu has launched the docuseries Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, which examines the mysterious deaths and disappearances of a group of male influencers in Thailand and focuses on the leader at the center of those events.
summary: The new Hulu docuseries Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death focuses on mysterious deaths and disappearances of male influencers in Thailand. It also highlights the leader at the center of those incidents.

content: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, began consulting with Heller—a public‑relations firm noted for handling sex‑scandal cases last year—in October 2025. The engagement coincided with the first reports linking Huang to a suspected Chinese spy.
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with consultants from Heller in October 2025. The hiring coincided with his first link to a suspected Chinese spy.

title: Sony to launch Japan‑only PlayStation Portal handheld with extra internal storage
content:
Sony is launching a new PlayStation Portal model exclusively in Japan next month. This updated handheld, available in the previously seen midnight black color, features “additional” internal storage intended for future functionality that Sony has not yet finalized. The device is restricted to Japanese language options and requires a PlayStation account registered in Japan.

The company is also renaming this specific Portal variant, though the full name is not provided in the source. Sony indicated it will announce the specific uses for the extra storage once the associated features are complete.
summary: Sony will release a new midnight‑black PlayStation Portal handheld in Japan next month. The model adds internal storage for future functionality, is locked to Japanese language and accounts, and will be renamed from PlayStation Portal Rem.
author: The Verge

title: Uber launches in-app Uber Parking service using SpotHero network
content:
Uber has introduced a new in‑app feature called Uber Parking that lets drivers locate, reserve, and pay for garage and lot spaces before they arrive. The service is built into the Uber app and is available through a new “Parking” icon.

The feature follows Uber’s recent acquisition of SpotHero, adding a network of more than 13,000 parking facilities in over 400 cities to the platform. Users can view an interactive map that displays upfront prices and arrival times, filter results by self‑park or valet, outdoor lot or garage, and whether staff are on‑site, and the app prompts drivers to enter their vehicle details and license plate.
summary: Uber launches in-app Uber Parking service using SpotHero network.
author: The Verge

title: Jensen Huang’s personal conduct tied to AI future and National Security Incident
content:
The Verge article references Jensen Huang in the context of a National Security Incident. It also discusses a separate matter involving Alice Huang, who is noted as a former TV reporter and is not related to Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang is described as an executive at Megaspeed, a company that has purchased $4.8 billion of hard‑to‑get Nvidia chips. The purchase began around the time that she was photographed with Jensen Huang in a Taipei bar in 2024.

The article notes that Megaspeed’s well‑funded push into AI appears to come out of nowhe, according to industry observers.
summary: Jensen Huang’s personal behavior is being linked to a National Security Incident and the future of AI. Alice Huang, a former TV reporter now an executive at Megaspeed, was photographed with him in a Taipei bar in 2024, and Megaspeed purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips.

title: James Gunn and Peter Safran to be replaced as DC Studios co-CEOs, remain producers
content: Soon, James Gunn and Peter Safran will no longer head up Skydance's DC Studios. After taking the helm of DC Studios as co-CEOs in 2022, Gunn and Safran are being replaced by former Marvel SVP of Production and Development Jeremy Latcham, Deadline reports. title: Instagram launches Effect Builder AI tool to create custom Story filters
content: After expanding its Edits app to macOS last week, Instagram's next move is launching this Effect Builder that generates custom filters for your Stories posts with AI. Available now for US residents who are over 18, it has a prompt box for describing your filter idea to the chatbot, with an option to attach style reference images. Then you can upload your own photos to preview the AI-generating effects, and ask for changes in follow-up prompts. There's also an option to allow Instagram's AI to rewrite your prompt, which turned my one-line test prompt "Make a filter that turns photos into comic book pages" into several AI-generated paragraphs …
summary: Instagram introduced an Effect Builder that uses AI prompts to generate custom filters for Stories posts. The feature is currently available to US residents over 18 and includes a prompt box, optional style images, photo previews, change requests, and an option for the AI to rewrite prompts.
author: The Verge

title: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate Three-Month Deal at $57.99 with Newegg Coupon
content:
Xbox Game Pass Ultimate has seen its monthly price range fluctuate between $20 and $30 over the past year. A recent promotion at Newegg offers a three‑month subscription for just $57.99 when the coupon code BNWF2656 is applied at checkout, bringing the effective monthly cost to roughly $19 per month.

The discount is achieved by subtracting $11 from the standard three‑month price, which is normally $68.99. After applying the coupon, the total cost for the three‑month plan is $57.99. This offer is available exclusively through Newegg and requires the use of the specified coupon code at the time of purchase.

The Ultimate plan provides full access to more than 500 games available on both Xbox consoles and Windows PC. In addition to the standard Game Pass library, subscribers receive EA Play and Ubisoft Plus Classics, each of which offers its own separate game libraries and benefits. The plan also includes Fortnite Crew, granting full access to the Fortnite battle passes, and enables online multiplayer on Xbox.

Over the last year, Microsoft has made several changes to the service that have altered its appeal. The plan was previously priced at $29.99 per month. Earlier in the year, the removal of Call of Duty titles from the library coincided with a price reduction to $22.99. More recently, Microsoft introduced hourly limits for cloud gaming; the Ultimate plan now includes 15 hours of cloud gaming per month, down from an unlimited allotment. These changes were announced shortly before the introduction of pay‑as‑you‑go plans for non‑Game Pass users.

In addition to the Game Pass deal, other discounted items are highlighted. The AMD Ryzen 7 9700X desktop CPU is offered at $269, a $70 discount from its usual price, and is compatible with AM5 motherboards. A Lego Pokémon Pikachu and Pokéball set is available for $159.95, a $40 discount on its standard price, featuring 2,050 pieces and standing 13.5 inches tall when assembled. The Bose Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar is marked down to $899, a $200 reduction, and includes Dolby Atmos, eARC over HDMI, Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth, and Alexa voice control. These offers provide additional value for gamers and tech enthusiasts.
summary: Newegg offers a three‑month Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscription for $57.99 when using coupon BNWF2656, reducing the monthly cost to about $19. The plan provides access to over 500 games, EA Play, Ubisoft Plus Classics, Fortnite Crew, and 15 cloud‑gaming hours per month.
author: The Verge

title: Anthropic unveils Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models
content:
Anthropic announced the release of two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, describing them as built to address “daunting” technical challenges. The company says the models improve on coding, reasoning and vision capabilities and generate outputs faster than the prior 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos series.

Claude Fable 5.2 is reported to excel at difficult software‑engineering tasks, coordinate agent teams and manage long‑running projects, and it has solved several complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical‑physics questions. Anthropic noted that the models underwent prerelease testing.
summary: Anthropic unveils Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models.
author: The Verge

title: Apple adds $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs to Logic Pro for extended AI access
content:
Apple has updated its Logic Pro application with an option to purchase "Intelligence Usage Packs" for a one-time fee of $49.99, according to a report by 9to5Mac. This feature follows a support article published in early September that detailed usage limits for specific Apple Intelligence capabilities. The packs enable users to continue accessing certain AI features that depend on cloud-based models from OpenAI or Google Gemini.

The built-in AI assistant within Logic Pro can perform tasks such as starting a new song, setting up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refining an active project. These usage limits apply because the features rely on external cloud-based AI models rather than on-device processing.
summary: Apple updated Logic Pro with a one‑time $49.99 “Buy More Usage” option for Intelligence Usage Packs. The packs let users keep using Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits tied to cloud‑based models from OpenAI or Google Gemini.
author: The Verge

title: Democrats likely to strip key component from Trump's Golden Dome missile shield
content:
Two senior Republican lawmakers who have supported the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile‑defense shield are set to leave Congress as a Democratic majority assumes control. Their departure has prompted questions about the future of President Donald Trump’s second‑term defense initiative, which he announced in January 2025, a week after beginning his second term.

Military officials have recently indicated they may retreat from one of Golden Dome’s key elements— the ability to intercept missiles during their initial boost phase shortly after launch. The program has faced little congressional examination since its announcement, but Democrats, now responsible for drafting the Pentagon budget, plan to impose funding limits and introduce legislation that would remove the controversial boost‑phase capability and rename the effort.
summary: Two leading Republican supporters of the Pentagon's Golden Dome missile defense are among the Republicans exiting Congress as Democrats prepare to assume control. Democrats intend to write the Pentagon budget, impose funding limits and introduce legislation to remove the boost‑phase missile‑intercept capability and rename the program.
author: Ars Technica

title: Rain‑soaked Brazilian Grand Prix delivers chaotic race as Norris shines
content:
The Brazilian Grand Prix delivered an unusually eventful race, according to the report. A mixed‑up starting order, fast drivers positioned toward the back of the grid and a track that alternated between drying and rain created abundant on‑track action.

Qualifying on Saturday was affected by rain, prompting drivers to use the wet‑weather tyre with deep treads. Although this tyre typically generates heavy spray that can force a suspension of running, the later knockout sessions featured fewer cars, allowing the session to continue without interruption.

Additional drama stemmed from grid penalties applied to Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari, each of whom had to use extra power‑unit components beyond the season’s allowance. These penalties altered the starting grid for the race.

The report also highlighted McLaren driver Lando Norris, the 2025 world champion, who displayed the form that earned him the title despite McLaren’s current difficulties in achieving race‑winning performance. Norris’s performance in Brazil was presented as a showcase of his championship‑winning ability.
summary: The Brazilian Grand Prix featured a wet‑dry‑wet track, a shuffled starting grid and grid penalties for Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton for using extra power‑unit components. McLaren’s Lando Norris, the 2025 champion, displayed the pace that earned him the title despite his team’s difficult‑to‑drive car.
author: Ars Technica

title: SpaceX VP Kiko Dontchev says company is now an infrastructure firm
content: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP. Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars." Read full article Comments
summary: At the UP Summit conference in Florida, SpaceX vice president of launch Kiko Dontchev said the company is now fundamentally an infrastructure company building ground and low‑Earth‑orbit infrastructure. He added that the Falcon 9 rocket is on the road to retirement as SpaceX pivots toward data, artificial intelligence and future Moon and Mars projects.
author: Ars Technica

title: Claude Code leaks thousands of secrets on public GitHub via settings file oversight
content: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ". Claude/settings. Local. Json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global. Gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly. Read full article Comments
summary: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
author: Ars Technica

title: Pentagon considers deploying fleet of military satellites in cislunar space
content: The US military has published a Request for Information on a federal procurement website signaling interest in deploying a "proliferated cislunar constellation" consisting of an unspecified number of satellites performing an undisclosed mission in the vicinity of the Moon. The announcement follows statements in recent months from the Space Force's acquisitions chief for advanced programs, Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, that the military was getting serious about extending its reach to the Moon. The Space Force's most distant satellites today are in geostationary orbit, some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, collecting routine surveillance and missile warning data. Most recently, Purdy spoke of a shift in Pentagon leadership's thinking about the Moon following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last December. The order set out the Trump administration's space policy. One section of the order deals with the US government's ability to detect, characterize, and counter threats to US space interests from low-Earth orbit to cislunar space, the term of art for the region of space around the Moon. Read full article Comments
summary: Pentagon considers deploying fleet of military satellites in cislunar space.
author: Ars Technica

title: Hackers exploit *sshole vulnerability to gain unauthenticated privileged access on Linux
content:
A newly disclosed critical vulnerability, identified as *sshole, enables attackers to log in to privileged accounts on a range of Linux systems. The flaw stems from the interaction between OpenSSH and the musl code library, and it affects Linux installations that use both components and satisfy additional unspecified conditions. Exploitation can grant unauthenticated access to high‑privilege accounts within seconds.

The vulnerability was made public last Thursday, prompting concerns about widespread Linux compromise. Four days later, security firm Greynoise reported that honeypots it operates in Southeast Asia were targeted by a group it labels GT10. Greynoise described the activity as “mature intrusions” and said it obtained access to a GT10 server, which revealed possible additional victims and the tools employed in the campaign. One of the backdoors used by the group contains Chinese‑language comments and appears to have been generated with artificial‑intelligence assistance.
summary: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl.
author: Ars Technica

title: Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy clouds Nvidia’s China ambitions
content: Jensen Huang is alleged to have had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The allegation, according to the report, could complicate Nvidia’s lobbying to ease U.S. chip export restrictions and to preserve its access to China’s AI market.
summary: Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy threatens to complicate Nvidia’s lobbying efforts to loosen U. S.
author: TechCrunch

title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3 billion after new financing round
content: Nominal, an AI platform for hardware engineering that lists Anduril as a major customer, has closed a new financing round that triples its valuation to $3 billion, an increase achieved within eight months. The funding round represents a significant boost in the startup’s market worth.
summary: Nominal, which offers an AI platform for hardware engineering and claims Anduril as a major customer, raised another big round of financing. The financing tripled the company's valuation to $3 billion.
author: TechCrunch

title: Grand Theft Auto becomes cultural colossus, showcased in Rockstar's London presentations
content: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong.
summary: Since its debut on PC and consoles in the late 1990s, Grand Theft Auto has challenged traditional game‑making conventions. In the 2000s Rockstar Games introduced new projects to UK writers in a London office, where presentations began with classic movie clips to set context.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Nvidia board urged to address succession planning amid Jensen Huang reliance
content: The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row? Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power. Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.
summary: Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation into an alleged honey‑trap spy scandal and faces criticism for not focusing on succession planning or key‑person risk. The chipmaker’s heavy reliance on founder‑CEO Jensen Huang, who holds a 3.6% stake and lacks super‑voting rights, is attracting business and political scrutiny.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Google says schools blocking its AI tools could lose access to Search, prompting criticism
content: Company says schools should control student AI use, but if they block its AI tools, they’ll lose access to search engine Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google’s announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search. Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google’s AI tools will also lose access to its search engine.
summary: Google announced new AI tools for schools and said teachers and administrators could restrict their use. The company warned that schools blocking its AI tools would also lose access to Google Search, drawing criticism from parents and teachers across the US.
author: Guardian Technology

title: AI leaders warn extinction risk even as superintelligence remains out of reach
content: The same technical limits that prevent superintelligence make these systems dangerous. But we know how to regulate them Many Silicon Valley leaders believe superintelligence is an imminent threat to society. The White House even published an accord about it. This isn’t enough. Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, estimates the risk of human extinction is at least 10% within the next few decades. The Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that unchecked AI “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems”. In response, 1,300 leaders and employees from many leading AI companies signed a letter calling to “deliberately pace” development.
summary: The same technical limits that prevent superintelligence make these systems dangerous. But we know how to regulate them Many Silicon Valley leaders believe superintelligence is an imminent threat to society.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Trump, Musk and Silicon Valley back Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid spy‑affair probe
content: Elon Musk and other finance moguls defend Jensen Huang after he admitted to the affair in an email to employees Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. “I have not ​spoken to him about it,” the US president told reporters on Sunday. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job”.
summary: Donald Trump, Elon Musk and other prominent finance moguls have expressed support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as he faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang admitted the affair in an email to employees, and Nvidia’s board is said to need to do some succession planning.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Palantir lobbied health minister Zubir Ahmed to extend AI tools to NHS GP records
content:
Palantir, the U.S. data‑analytics firm, used a direct WhatsApp channel to press health minister Zubir Ahmed MP to consider extending the company’s artificial‑intelligence technology to General Practitioner (GP) records. In the messages, Palantir argued that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and described its software as “ideal” for that purpose.

The lobbying effort took place in February, even though GP data had been expressly excluded from the scope of Palantir’s existing £330 million contract with NHS England for its federated data platform (FDP). The company says the FDP has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays. Palantir was co‑founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, identified in the report as a Trump‑supporting figure.
summary: WhatsApp messages show Palantir pressed MP Zubir Ahmed to help bring sensitive GP data onto its platform. The lobbying occurred in February despite GP data being expressly excluded from Palantir’s existing £330m NHS England contract for its federated data platform.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Women protest in Manila demand “Trump out” ahead of 49th ASEAN summit
content: Women protesters marched in Manila on Monday, 9 November, before Donald Trump’s visit for the 49th ASEAN summit. Demonstrators carried “Trump Out” signs and also voiced opposition to a U.S.–led initiative on semiconductors and critical minerals.
summary: Women protesters took to the streets of Manila on Monday 9 November ahead of Donald Trump's visit for the 49th ASEAN summit. They carried “Trump Out” placards and denounced a US‑led initiative on semiconductors and critical minerals.
author: Euronews

title: Seven killed, 125 injured in Egypt train collision south of Cairo
content: Two passenger trains collided south of Cairo, killing seven people and injuring at least 125 others. On Monday 9 November, rail workers began repairing the damaged tracks in Al‑Ayyat, Egypt, the day after the crash.
summary: Two passenger trains collided south of Cairo, killing seven people and injuring at least 125 others. Rail workers began repairing the damaged tracks in Al-Ayyat on Monday 9 November.
author: Euronews

title: Ukraine damages three units at Russia's KINEF refinery, 7% of capacity
content: Ukraine struck the KINEF plant, Russia’s second‑largest refinery, damaging three main processing units. The facility handles roughly 7 % of Russia’s refining capacity and supplies fuel to St Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport. Rosneft subsequently capped fuel sales in six regions, limiting city drivers to 30 litres per transaction.
summary: Three main processing units at the KINEF plant, which handles about 7% of Russia’s refining capacity and supplies St Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport, were damaged. Rosneft capped fuel sales in six regions, limiting drivers to 30 litres per transaction in cities.
author: Euronews

title: IIHF moves Norway to Division 1A to free spot for Russia in Alberta junior tournament
content: The International Ice Hockey Federation has shifted Norway, the world’s 10th‑ranked junior team, to Division 1A to open a slot for Russia at the upcoming tournament in Alberta. The move follows a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling that ordered Russian teams reinstated, though the adjustment remains unconfirmed and Russian players have not yet secured Canadian visas.
summary: The IIHF moved Norway, ranked 10th, to Division 1A to free a spot for Russia at the junior tournament in Alberta after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordered Russian teams reinstated. The change has not been confirmed and Russia has not been guaranteed Canadian visas.
author: Euronews

title: Pope Leo XIV welcomed by crowds in Claypole during South American tour
content: Pope Leo XIV was welcomed by crowds in Claypole, a town near Buenos Aires, during a visit to the Don Orione care home. While there, the pontiff greeted the faithful and unveiled a plaque as part of his 12‑day South American tour.
summary: Pope Leo XIV was welcomed by crowds in Claypole, near Buenos Aires, as he visited the Don Orione care home. He greeted the faithful and unveiled a plaque during his 12‑day South American tour.
author: Euronews

title: Pope Leo XIV urges Milei government to protect vulnerable after Cottolengo visit
content: The Pontiff, Pope Leo XIV, visited the Cottolengo Don Orione facility in Argentina, which serves more than 400 people and has been affected by budget cuts attributed to President Javier Milei’s government. During the visit he said a nation’s progress should be measured by how it treats its most vulnerable citizens, urging the administration to protect them.
summary: The Pope visited the Cottolengo Don Orione, a centre that cares for over 400 people and has been hit by cuts from Javier Milei’s government. He said a nation’s progress should be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable and urged Milei’s government to protect them.
author: Euronews

title: Nvidia shares drop over 8% as board launches probe into CEO Jensen Huang
content: Nvidia’s stock fell more than eight percent in early Monday trading after the company disclosed that its board has launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang following reports he was targeted by Chinese intelligence. The probe will be conducted by a committee of independent directors with assistance from outside counsel.
summary: Shares of artificial intelligence leader Nvidia fell more than eight percent in early Monday trading after the company said it was launching an investigation of CEO Jensen Huang. The board announced a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will conduct the probe following reports that Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence.
author: France 24

title: French PM Sebastien Lecornu moves minimum wage hike to December
content: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said ​on Monday, November 9, he was bringing forward a planned hike in the minimum wage to December from January, as he sought to defuse a cost-of-living crisis that has sparked some of France's worst civil unrest in years. Unions swiftly dismissed the offer as "crumbs".
summary: French PM Sebastien Lecornu moves minimum wage hike to December.
author: France 24

title: Economist Renaud Foucart says France's 1.6% wage rise won't end election protests
content:
Annette Young welcomed Renaud Foucart, a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Economics ECARES at Lancaster University, to discuss the current state of social unrest in France.  

Foucart noted that France’s recent 1.6 % increase in the minimum wage was introduced in response to nationwide protests. While the raise may provide a temporary relief from social unrest, it does not address the deeper political and institutional crisis the country faces.  

According to Foucart, the core issue extends beyond declining purchasing power, fiscal constraints and the limitations of a minority government. He argues that the protests are driven by a growing loss of faith in politics itself. “They are in the street because they don’t believe politics can achieve anything,” Foucart said, suggesting that the persistence of mass demonstrations ahead of the presidential election reflects profound disillusionment with the political system’s capacity to deliver meaningful change.
summary: Annette Young welcomed Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer in the Department of Economics ECARES at Lancaster University. He said the 1.6% minimum‑wage increase may offer a temporary reprieve but does little to resolve the deeper loss of faith in politics fueling protests ahead of the presidential election.
author: France 24

title: NRC adviser says life in Gaza miserable amid flooding and aid restrictions
content: Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Shaina Low, Communication Adviser for the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). Thirteen months into what she describes as a "so-called ceasefire," the humanitarian crisis in Gaza continues to deepen, exposing the profound gap between diplomatic commitments and the lived realities of Palestinian civilians. In an interview with France 24, Shayna Low, communications adviser in Palestine for the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), describes a population confronting winter flooding, repeated displacement, deteriorating shelter conditions and persistent restrictions on humanitarian assistance. "Life in Gaza is simply miserable." Low urges Israel to "open all the crossings, lift the restrictions, let aid in."
summary: NRC adviser says life in Gaza miserable amid flooding and aid restrictions.
author: France 24

title: French protesters rally against austerity as nation hosts G7 foreign ministers
content:
France, known for haute couture and high‑speed rail, is grappling with an affordability issue even as it remains the world’s seventh largest economy.  

This week, France’s top diplomat hosted a Group of Seven Industrialized Nations foreign ministers meeting inside the regal setting of its landmark Left Bank ministry.
summary: Protesters in France are raging against austerity measures. France, with the planet’s seventh largest economy, is hosting a Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting at its Left Bank ministry.
author: France 24

title: France probes Iranian Revolutionary Guard cyber unit after supermarket fridge attacks
content:
France announced on Monday that it has opened a probe into Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, accusing the unit of carrying out “unprecedented” cyberattacks on supermarket fridges across the country. The French government said it would impose sanctions on a European level against Tehran in response.

The attacks, which occurred on October 11 and 12, targeted swathes of French supermarkets. They raised the temperatures inside refrigerators, forcing some stores to discard entire inventories of perishable food.
summary: France said Iran's Revolutionary Guards carried out unprecedented cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators on October 11 and 12, raising temperatures and causing many stores to discard perishable food. The French government opened a probe and pledged to seek European‑level sanctions against Tehran.
author: France 24

title: Egyptian FM Badr Abdelatty says Iran and US want to negotiate, urges concrete deal
content:
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told FRANCE 24 that he believes both Iran and the United States are interested in negotiating.  He urged the parties to reach a “concrete deal” to avert another escalation.  

Abdelatty also said Cairo remains “counting” on U.S. President Donald Trump to advance the stalled Gaza peace plan and expressed confidence that U.S. military aid to Egypt will continue.
summary: Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said he believed Iran and the United States wanted to negotiate and called for a concrete deal to prevent another escalation. He said Cairo is still counting on President Donald Trump to move forward with the stalled Gaza peace plan and is confident US military aid to Egypt will continue.
author: France 24

title: Rep. Thomas Massie moves to force House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
content: Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie moved on Monday to force a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The action pressures other Republicans to consider removing the former Trump administration official following the party’s recent midterm election losses.
summary: Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie moved on Monday to force a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The action puts pressure on fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove the Trump administration figure after the party's crushing midterm defeat.
author: France 24

title: EU plans to select new ECB chief by end of December
content: The European Union says it expects to choose a new European Central Bank chief by the end of December, after Christine Lagarde announced she will step down early as ECB head, creating a tight schedule for the appointment.
summary: Christine Lagarde decided to step down early as head of the European Central Bank. The European Union expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of December.
author: DW World

title: Iran leverages Strait of Hormuz attacks to influence energy shipping costs
content: Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are endangering crews and raising the cost of energy shipping. The extent to which Iran can maintain these attacks, together with the limits of U.S. protection, will determine how much trade can continue through the waterway and at what price.
summary: Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz put crews at risk and raise energy shipping costs. Iran's ability to sustain the attacks and the limits of US protection will shape how much trade can continue and at what price.
author: DW World

title: African nations intensify fight against fake news amid free‑speech concerns
content: Across Africa—from Ghana to Mozambique—the fight against fake news is gaining momentum. At the same time, efforts to curb disinformation are raising concerns about free‑speech safeguards, a dynamic that places some governments in an inconvenient position.
summary: The fight against fake news is gaining momentum across countries from Ghana to Mozambique. Efforts to combat disinformation are raising concerns about free‑speech safeguards and putting some governments in an inconvenient position.
author: DW World

title: Security Council meets on Ukraine as Russian strikes threaten power grid
content: The United Nations Security Council convened in New York to discuss Ukraine, noting that recent Russian strikes on the country’s energy infrastructure are endangering millions with the prospect of a cold, dark winter and that civilian deaths are rising sharply. The session was held on the eve of U.S.-backed peace talks scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi.
summary: The Security Council is meeting in New York to discuss Ukraine as Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure. The attacks threaten millions with a cold, dark winter and civilian deaths are rising sharply ahead of US‑backed peace talks in Abu Dhabi.
author: UN News

title: IOM calls for urgent funding for tens of thousands of Ethiopian refugees in Kenya's Moyale
content: The International Organization of Migration (IOM) and its partners are urging urgent funding to aid tens of thousands of families who have fled violent clashes in Ethiopia and taken refuge in Kenya’s Moyale region. The displaced people need food, water and shelter.
summary: The International Organization of Migration and partners are seeking urgent funding. The money would support tens of thousands of people who escaped violent clashes in Ethiopia and are now in the Moyale region of northern Kenya.
author: UN News

title: COP31 opens in Antalya as nearly 200 nations seek concrete climate decisions
content: COP31 opened on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast in Antalya, drawing nearly 200 countries. Delegates emphasized a shift toward concrete decisions rather than broad declarations, confronting challenges on climate finance, clean‑energy deployment and protection for communities already affected by climate change. The summit’s agenda is heightened by a strong El Niño that threatens to intensify extreme weather.
summary: Nearly 200 countries have arrived on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast for the COP31 climate summit. Negotiators are confronting tough questions on climate finance, clean energy and protecting communities as a powerful El Niño threatens to worsen extreme weather.
author: UN News

title: Teddy Riner, five‑time Olympic judo champion, announces bid for French presidency
content:
France’s most celebrated athlete, five‑time Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner, announced his intention to run in next year’s presidential election. Riner said he is “neither leftwing nor rightwing” and would aim to “bring people together” if elected.

The vote, scheduled for April‑May, will determine Emmanuel Macron’s successor. Current polling shows a weakening political centre, with anti‑immigrant National Rally leader Marine Le Pen positioned as a possible frontrunner and radical‑left candidate Jean‑Luc Mélenchon trailing.
summary: Teddy Riner, five‑time Olympic judo champion, announces bid for French presidency.
author: Guardian World

title: France says Iran behind cyber‑attack on supermarket freezers, vows EU sanctions
content: French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”. Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”.
summary: France says Iran was responsible for a massive cyber‑attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that took control of digital thermostats and raised temperatures above 50 °C. French foreign minister Jean‑Noël Barrot announced Europe‑wide sanctions against those responsible.
author: Guardian World

title: Iran‑attributed hack disrupts French supermarket freezers, linked to broader attacks
content:
A defrosting hack that disrupted French supermarket freezers has been described as “not particularly complex” and attributed to Iranian actors, with analysts presuming it is linked to similar incidents across Europe. The attribution reflects a broader pattern in which Iranian‑linked hackers are said to use cyber operations to send political messages.

The report notes earlier Iranian‑affiliated activity in 2023, including a state‑backed group that interrupted television streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deep‑fake report on the Gaza war, and another incident where hackers displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water‑control equipment produced by an Israeli firm.
summary: A defrosting hack that disrupted French supermarket freezers has been attributed to Iran and is thought to be linked to other attacks across Europe. Iranian‑linked hackers have previously interrupted UAE TV streaming with a deep‑fake Gaza report and displayed a “down with Israel” slogan on Israeli water‑control equipment.
author: Guardian World

title: Treasurer Jim Chalmers faces pressure to cut home battery subsidies in mid-year budget
content:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is facing heightened pressure to curb spending as part of a mid‑year budget update aimed at fighting inflation. The Treasury’s focus has turned to green‑energy subsidies, with the most intense scrutiny on the home‑battery scheme that, since July last year, has provided a taxpayer‑backed 30 % rebate to households and businesses.  

The same Treasury review also places electric‑vehicle incentives and home‑battery rebates under scrutiny, while noting that scaling back nuclear‑powered submarine funding and diesel‑fuel rebates for miners is presented as a stronger economic case for cuts.
summary: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is under increasing pressure to fight inflation by cutting spending in the mid-year budget update, with calls to slash Labor’s green energy subsidies for households. The cheaper home batteries program, offering a 30% taxpayer‑backed rebate to households and businesses since July last year, is receiving the most focus.
author: Guardian World

title: Australian Institute of Criminology report finds Queensland police deprioritise rape cases
content: Prosecutors dropped cases because survivors ‘didn’t act how a rape victim should’, Australian Institute of Criminology review of 19,000 sexual assault cases finds Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Queensland police put sexual assault investigations “on the backburner” because detectives were overworked and under pressure to prioritise cases linked to political issues such as youth crime, a major new study has found The report, published this month by the Australian Institute of Criminology, sought to investigate why so many sexual assault complaints – about two-thirds of those made to police in Queensland – were withdrawn, not substantiated or considered unsolved.
summary: A review of 19,000 Queensland sexual assault cases found prosecutors dropped cases because survivors did not act as expected of rape victims. The report said Queensland police put many investigations on the backburner due to overworked detectives and pressure to prioritize politically linked cases such as youth crime.
author: Guardian World

title: ACT police criticised by magistrate for tasering disabled Aboriginal woman
content: Exclusive: Body-worn camera footage shows woman pulled off bench and a Taser activated despite ‘putting up no resistance’, magistrate says Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast A magistrate has criticised “exceedingly heavy-handed” ACT police officers who Tasered an Aboriginal woman with an intellectual disability during a routine arrest. The woman, named Emma, pleaded with officers not to use the stun gun on her and told them she was unarmed during the arrest at a Canberra bus stop in January.
summary: A magistrate said ACT police were “exceedingly heavy‑handed” after they tasered an Aboriginal woman with an intellectual disability. The woman, identified as Emma, told officers she was unarmed and begged them not to use the stun gun during a routine arrest at a Canberra bus stop in January.
author: Guardian World

title: UN climate chief Simon Stiell says high fossil fuel prices spread inflation like cancer
content:
UN climate chief Simon Stiell opened the summit in Turkey with a plenary address, warning that a global fossil‑fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet. He delivered the remarks at the opening session of the critical UN climate talks hosted in Turkey.

Stiell joined the Cop31 hosts, Turkey and Australia, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an alternative to continued reliance on oil, coal and gas. Australia is leading the negotiations.
summary: Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief, said a global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” during the opening plenary of COP31 in Turkey. He joined Turkey and Australia, the COP31 hosts, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an alternative to oil, coal and gas.
author: Guardian World

title: Deadly flash floods in Erbil, Iraq kill two as thunderstorms dump 80mm rain
content:
Violent thunderstorms swept across northern Iraq and parts of Iran on Saturday, generating deadly flash floods. The same weather system also produced strong winds in Portugal and prompted Japan to brace for additional snowfall.

In Erbil, the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan, the flooding was severe. Homes and businesses suffered extensive damage, and streets were inundated by torrential rain that fell in a very short period.

Rainfall in Erbil exceeded expectations, with an estimated 80 mm falling compared to the forecasted 30 mm. The deluge killed two people.
summary: Deadly flash floods struck northern Iraq, especially Erbil, on Saturday after severe thunderstorms swept the region and also affected parts of Iran. The floods killed two people and caused extensive damage to homes and businesses, with about 80 mm of rain falling in Erbil, far above the forecasted 30 mm.
author: Guardian World

title: Ramla Ali wins WBO and IBF junior featherweight titles in controversial split decision
content:
British-Somali boxer Ramla Ali became a world champion for the first time at age 36, securing a split decision victory over former sparring partner Mikiah Kreps in Arlington, Texas. The 10-round bout, held at the College Park Center, awarded Ali the vacant WBO and IBF women’s junior featherweight titles. The result was described as highly contentious, with reports indicating that Kreps outlanded Ali but ultimately lost the disputed decision despite appearing to control much of the fight.

Ali’s victory marked her second attempt at a world championship, completing her rise to the top of the 122lb division. She grew up in east London after fleeing Somalia’s civil war with her family and became the first boxer to represent the African country at the Olympics. The article also notes that Australia’s Nicolson retained the junior featherweight title, while other results included Baumgardner winning the 135lb belt amid a heating feud with Dubois.
summary: British-Somali boxer Ramla Ali won the vacant WBO and IBF women's junior featherweight titles at age 36 after a highly contentious 10‑round split decision over former sparring partner Mikiah Kreps at College Park Center in Arlington, Texas. The decision was disputed, with many observers saying Kreps had controlled the bout.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Les Kiss Still Unsettled Over Wallabies Fly‑Half After England Defeat
content:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss continues to search for a solution to his team’s ongoing issues at the fly-half position following a heavy defeat to England at Twickenham. The article highlights the difficulty of filling this role, noting that seven different players have started at No 10 since the 2023 World Cup. That tournament ended in ignominy for Australia, which crashed out at the group stage before Eddie Jones lost his job.

Noah Lolesio, who had 12 Test starts in that period—more than double the next man—was the incumbent until he was stretchered off against Fiji in the run-up to the British & Irish Lions series last year. Now fit again and only 26, Lolesio is currently representing Toyota Industries Corporation Shuttles Aichi in Japan. The piece draws a comparison to the struggle of filling the Defence Against the Dark Arts post at Hogwarts, suggesting that Kiss is the latest Wallabies coach desperate for a stable answer at first receiver.
summary: Les Kiss Still Unsettled Over Wallabies Fly‑Half After England Defeat.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Joe Burrow leads Bengals to 6-2 record, eyes MVP race
content:
Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow has emerged as a strong contender for the MVP award after leading his team to four consecutive victories. The Bengals recently defeated the Atlanta Falcons 34-17 at the Santiago Bernabéu stadium in Madrid, improving their record to 6-2. This surge in performance marks a significant turnaround for the franchise, which had a combined regular-season record of 24-27 and no playoff appearances from 2023 through 2025 due to injuries and defensive struggles.

Burrow’s recent statistical output has placed him in elite company. Over the last four weeks, he has thrown 16 touchdown passes, the most in a four-game span in Bengals history, which dates back to 1968. He is currently the second quarterback in professional football history to record 16 or more passing touchdowns and two or more rushing touchdowns in any four-game span, joining Tom Brady from the 2007 season. That 2007 campaign saw the New England Patriots’ offense average 36.8 points per game.

The improvement in Burrow’s performance is also reflected in the protection he receives from his offensive line. This season, he has been pressured on just 30.2% of his dropbacks, a notable decrease from the 33.8% pressure rate in 2025 and the 34.2% rate in 2024. This enhanced protection contributes to the team’s current momentum as they distance themselves in the MVP race.
summary: The quarterback has led Cincinnati to four straight wins with stat lines that put him in the company of Tom Brady. At this rate, the trophy seems his to lose At the end of the 2021 season, the Cincinnati Bengals came up three points short in Super Bowl LVI against the Los Angeles Rams.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Warner says 100% accurate that all players knew of sandpaper plot, backs Khawaja

summary: David Warner, former vice‑captain, says it is “100% accurate” that every player knew of the sandpaper plot and gives “full support” to Usman Khawaja. He also claims Cricket Australia’s investigation was “rushed and botched”, according to a video posted on Monday.

title: ‘I’m going to tell the truth. Screw this!’ Billie Jean King at 82 on coming out, tearing up tennis – and her one big regret
content:
Billie Jean King, now 82, reflects on a lifetime of achievements while still competing at the highest level. She recalls her historic battle for equal prize money, her continued tenacity on the court, and her recent graduation from college. King also discusses her sexuality, describing how coming out has shaped her life.

In a daily exercise, King compiles a “gratitude list” in her mind. Today’s list includes her nephew, her wife Ilana Kloss—who, like King, is a decorated former tennis player—and Susan Williams, who was in King’s fifth‑grade class in Long Beach, California. Williams was the first person to ask, “Do you want to play tennis?” and to explain the sport as a mix of running, jumping, and hitting a ball.

King’s early childhood was marked by athletic encouragement from her parents, who supported her sporting ambitions as much as her brother’s. Her brother later became a Major League Baseball pitcher. Although basketball was a major part of her early years, it was Williams who introduced her to tennis, a game that quickly became one of her favorite activities.
summary: ‘I’m going to tell the truth. Screw this!’ Billie Jean King at 82 on coming out, tearing up tennis – and her one big regret.

content:

title: US Lacks Official Delegation at COP31, Democrats Seek to Reclaim Climate Role
content: US government will have no official presence at UN’s annual climate summit, this year’s Cop31 held in Antalya, Turkey The US will be absent from key UN climate talks that start on Monday, a further sign of Donald Trump’s scornful dismissal of the climate crisis. But Democrats’ crushing win in the US midterm elections has delivered a timely shot of optimism to countries now looking beyond the Trump era of climate obstruction. For the second year in a row, there will be no official US government presence at the annual climate summit, this year known as Cop31 and held in Antalya, Turkey. While almost every other country in the world sends delegations to the talks, Trump has derided the climate crisis as a “hoax” and “bullshit” and triggered the withdrawal of the US from the entire international climate framework.
summary: The US government will have no official presence at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, for the second consecutive year. Democrats, buoyed by a midterm election victory, hope to reverse the Trump-era climate withdrawal.

title: MIT/NYU FLEX platform lets robots infer higher-level intent from natural language
content:
MIT and New York University researchers have unveiled FLEX, a flexible feature‑editing pipeline that lets robots interpret natural, conversational language commands and extend those instructions beyond their literal wording. The system was presented this month at the annual Conference on Robot Learning and is designed to improve robot motion‑planning by allowing a human to give high‑level directives that the robot can reason about and apply to its environment.

In a series of simulated trials, a virtual robotic arm was tasked with moving objects such as a cup of coffee, a candle, and a bowling ball. Participants typed commands like “Don’t spill on my laptop,” “Stay away from the stack of paper,” or “Don’t drop on the mug.” FLEX enabled the robot to follow each instruction literally while also inferring broader rules—avoiding electronics, flammable items, and fragile objects—without the user having to list every detail.

The core of FLEX is a large language model, GPT‑4o, which the robot consults during the “Generalize” step. The model scans its extensive training data to find patterns linking the user’s specified features (e.g., a laptop or a mug) to related categories such as electronics or fragile items. This common‑sense reasoning allows the robot to add new constraints automatically.

FLEX operates in three phases that take roughly five seconds. First, “Add” places the user‑identified feature on a list of relevant objects. Second, “Generalize” uses the LLM to expand that list based on learned associations. Third, “Mask” employs the robot’s vision system to remove objects that are no longer present, keeping the feature list current.

The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT, with co‑authors Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University. Bobu directs MIT’s Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, which focuses on autonomous agents that can learn and adapt to human preferences. The work received partial support from the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium and the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing’s Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing program.
summary: MIT and New York University researchers introduced FLEX, a flexible feature‑editing pipeline that lets robots interpret natural language commands and generalize to avoid electronics, fragile items, and other hazards. The platform, demonstrated in simulated scenarios such as a robot serving coffee, was presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning.

title: WorldParticle: MIT-UBC AI model simulates multiple physical phenomena
content:
A new deep‑learning system called WorldParticle is being presented as a single AI model that can simulate a wide range of physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins. The work is the result of a collaboration among researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the University of British Columbia (UBC), and several other institutions. The team describes the model as a “foundation model” for simulation that could replace the current practice of building separate, hand‑coded solvers for each type of material or process.

WorldParticle represents any material as a collection of tiny three‑dimensional particles using a Lagrangian formulation. A neural network receives the particles’ positions and physical properties as inputs and predicts their positions and properties for the next simulation step. The system separates external forces, makes an initial prediction, and then reintegrates those forces to correct the particle states, allowing it to adapt to new materials, forces, and environments that were not part of its training set.

To keep the computation tractable when objects are broken into millions of particles, the researchers incorporated a merging technique that compresses particles while preserving fine‑grained detail. The model was tested on six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects, granular materials and protein dynamics. In these tests WorldParticle achieved higher accuracy than conventional numerical simulators; for example, it correctly captured the collapse of a granular pile where baseline methods left particles floating, and it simulated protein structural changes about 100 times faster than existing numerical approaches.

The research team, led by Peter Yichen Chen (assistant professor at UBC) and Minghao Guo (MIT postdoc), includes graduate students Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, MIT professor Wojciech Matusik, and collaborators from Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, UCLA and the University of Hong Kong. The findings will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia. The authors envision extending WorldParticle to additional domains such as soft‑robot manipulation, RNA evolution and astrophysical processes, with the longer‑term goal of creating a general‑purpose simulation pipeline for scientific discovery.
summary: Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves.

title: 2026 Antarctic ozone hole reaches seventh‑largest area on September 18
content:
The NASA Earth Observatory has released a new data visualization that shows the area and shape of the Antarctic ozone hole on September 18, 2026, the day the hole reaches its annual maximum extent. Scientists define the ozone hole as the region where ozone concentrations fall below the historical threshold of 220 Dobson units (DU). The image, produced by Lauren Dauphin, is part of an update to the Observatory’s “World of Change” series that documents how Earth changes over time.

The visualization is based on satellite measurements taken from 1979 through 2026. From 1979‑2004 the data came from NASA’s Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer (TOMS) on Nimbus‑7 and other satellites; from 2005‑2011 the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) on the Aura satellite was used; from 2012‑2025 the Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS) on the Suomi NPP satellite provided the data; and in 2026 OMPS on the NOAA‑20 satellite supplied the latest observations. The map shows red and yellow areas indicating the ozone hole, with the word “hole” used metaphorically because no place is truly empty of ozone.

The 2026 hole was the seventh largest in the 48‑year record of monitoring, measured by its mean size from September 7 to October 13, the peak ozone‑depletion season. It was not as deep as some of the larger holes on record, but an unusually strong Antarctic polar vortex created ideal conditions for ozone depletion over a large area. Year‑to‑year variations in the hole’s area and depth are driven by changes in stratospheric temperature and circulation; colder conditions produce a larger area and lower ozone values in the core of the hole.

The Observatory’s article traces the history of the ozone hole, noting that before 1979 no ozone concentrations below 220 DU had been observed. In 1985, ground‑based measurements at Halley Research Station first reported dramatic thinning of the Antarctic stratosphere, and NASA satellite data revealed the continental scale of the depletion. The hole’s depth fell below 100 DU for the first time in 1991, and the deepest hole occurred in 1994 when concentrations dropped to 73 DU. The longest‑recorded largest hole occurred in 2006.

The article also summarizes the broader context of ozone‑depleting substances. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released into the troposphere persist for decades and, once reaching the stratosphere, break apart under ultraviolet light to release chlorine, which catalyzes ozone destruction. Human‑produced chlorine accounts for about 80 % of the chlorine in the stratosphere today, while bromine compounds also contribute. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased out the production of these chemicals, and satellite evidence from 2018 showed a 20 % decrease in ozone depletion during the Antarctic winter months from 2005 to 2016. Models predict that the Antarctic ozone layer will return to 1980 levels in the 2070s.
summary: The Antarctic ozone hole reached its annual maximum area on September 18, 2026, measured by the OMPS instrument on the NOAA‑20 satellite. The 2026 hole was the seventh‑largest in 48 years of monitoring, though its depth was less than that of other large holes on record.

title: APOD November 9 2026 – Rigel and the Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118)
content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 9 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Rigel and the Witch Head Nebula Explanation: Does the blue nebula look like the head of a witch? The nebula is known popularly as the Witch Head Nebula because, it is said, the nebula’s shape resembles a Halloween-style caricature of a witch’s head. Exactly how, though, can be a topic of imaginative speculation. What is clear is that IC 2118 is about 50 light-years across and made of gas and dust that points to — because it has been partly eroded by — the nearby star Rigel. One of the brighter stars in the constellation Orion, Rigel lies just below the center of the featured image. The blue color of the Witch Head Nebula and is caused not only by Rigel’s intense blue starlight but also because the dust grains scatter blue light more efficiently than red. The same physical process causes Earth’s daytime sky to appear blue, although the scatterers in planet Earth’s atmosphere are molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. title: Flide inference engine speeds Jev-like decision models up to 9.5× faster
content:
Flide is a new inference engine designed specifically for Jev‑like decision models. The developers say that decision models require their own inference engine, so they created Flide to provide high‑performance, exact inference for this class of models.

According to the announcement, Flide delivers up to a 9.5‑fold speed improvement over the popular vLLM and SGLang engines. It also supports more than 30 widely used local Jev‑like decision models.

Users can install Flide immediately with `pip install flide`. The Show HN post (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50421155) has 25 points and 4 comments.

title: England hospitals at 95% adult bed occupancy during peak flu season
content:
The piece warns that relentless streamlining can create hidden dangers, using England’s hospital capacity as a case in point. During the peak of last year’s flu season, about 95 % of adult hospital beds were occupied, a level that would be praised as efficient if hospitals were treated like hotels.  

The article argues that such high occupancy leaves little reserve capacity, meaning a single severe flu week could force treatment to be shifted into corridors. It suggests that the drive to optimise every system—from traffic roundabouts to financial markets—may backfire when it eliminates the buffers needed to handle unexpected spikes in demand.
summary: In England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year. The article warns that such high occupancy leaves little reserve capacity and could force treatment in corridors.

title: ‘Thicky thicky dumb dumb’ satirist Cody Dahler on his viral videos: ‘my material is presented to me on a silver platter!’
content: The writer and podcaster on why politics is made to seem more complicated than it is and his mission to unpack world events for everyone Why did you get into comedy? My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else. Where do you find your material? In a world where Robert Jenrick claims Nigel Farage has “ probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism ”, the answer is that my material is presented to me on a silver platter each morning.
summary: The writer and podcaster on why politics is made to seem more complicated than it is and his mission to unpack world events for everyone Why did you get into comedy? My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform.

title: MP Ben Coleman urges NHS not to extend Palantir contract ending March
content:
Labour MP Ben Coleman, who represents Chelsea and Fulham and sits on the health and social care committee, warned that public confidence in Palantir is low and argued that the NHS should move away from its reliance on the U.S. firm. He noted that Palantir’s £330 million contract to operate NHS England’s federated data platform is set to expire next March, and that ministers must decide by Christmas whether to extend the agreement.

Coleman said the committee recommended no extension, citing contested benefits and the availability of alternative tools that could provide similar functionality. He urged a transition to new suppliers that would give the NHS full control of its technology and patient data. While acknowledging the appeal of appointing a single British firm, he cautioned that such a choice would not guarantee the NHS the flexibility to change suppliers without losing the systems it has built.
summary: MP Ben Coleman urges NHS not to extend Palantir contract ending March.

summary: Daryna, 25, lives in Kyiv where her days are marked by air raid alerts, power outages and nights sheltering in the subway since Russia’s full-scale invasion. title: Gen Z protests challenge authoritarianism in Brazil, Serbia and worldwide
content:
Young people in Serbia, Bangladesh, India, France and Brazil are confronting what they see as authoritarianism and altering political dynamics. In Brazil, activists organized massive online rallies, sharing videos and memes, while Serbian youths travelled by bicycle across Europe and completed ultramarathons to amplify their message.

Both the Serbian and Brazilian actions entered the international spotlight last month, becoming focal points in election campaigns that highlighted resistance to authoritarian rule. Observers describe these developments as part of a broader, worldwide pattern of youth‑led movements reshaping political landscapes.
summary: From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
