title: Reece Walsh shines as Australia reaches Rugby League World Cup final
content: On a fractious night in Sydney, Australia secured a place in another Men’s Rugby League World Cup final. The match put Reece Walsh at the centre of attention, drawing both praise and criticism for his role in the semi‑final.
summary: The semi‑final in Sydney ended with Australia advancing to another Men's Rugby League World Cup final. Reece Walsh was a central figure in the match, drawing both praise and criticism.
author: BBC Sport

title: Democrats aim to end Iran war with some Republican support
content: Democrats, buoyed by the recent midterm surge, say they intend to halt President Trump’s war with Iran after they regain a Senate majority next year. Senate Democrats claim they have some Republican backing for ending the conflict, which has persisted for more than eight months, and have warned they will use their “power…” to pursue that goal.
summary: Senate Democrats say they will try to halt President Trump’s war with Iran after regaining the Senate majority next year. They claim some Republican backing and have threatened to use congressional power to end the conflict that has dragged on for over eight months.
author: The Hill

title: Trump posts Family Guy‑style cartoon of UFC boss Dana White as press secretary
content: President Trump on Sunday shared a cartoon of UFC CEO Dana White as White House press secretary after announcing that White had been proposed as a candidate for the role. The president posted a cartoon video with the same animation style as “Family Guy.” In the video, White is in the White House briefing room,…
summary: President Trump on Sunday shared a cartoon video that depicts UFC CEO Dana White as a White House press secretary. The video uses a “Family Guy” animation style and shows White in the White House briefing room.
author: The Hill

title: Ex-RFK Jr adviser requests records on Wiles’s health policy influence
content: Calley Means, who previously served as a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has asked that records documenting former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s influence on health policy be retained. He made the request after alleging that Wiles caused the Trump administration to repeatedly defer to corporate interests in health‑policy decisions.
summary: Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., requested records on former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’s health policy influence be preserved following allegations he made that she led the Trump administration to consistently bow to corporate interests on health policy.
author: The Hill

title: Sen. Bernie Sanders says Democrats must hold Trump accountable but not focus only on investigations
content: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I‑Vt.) said on Sunday that Democrats, upon assuming control of Congress in January, must hold President Trump accountable, but warned they “cannot spend all of our time” solely investigating the president, questioning whether the focus should be on the administration’s alleged corruption and illegal, unconstitutional actions.
summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) on Sunday said Democrats will need to hold President Trump accountable when they take over control of Congress starting in January but added that they “cannot spend all of our time” just investigating the president.
author: The Hill

title: AI nearly caused US troops to attack Chinese ship, exposing oversight gaps
content: The lack of independent oversight and verifiable records in artificial intelligence deployment poses significant risks to national security, finance and healthcare, necessitating a solution similar to aviation's flight recorders.
summary: AI nearly prompted US troops to attack a Chinese ship. The episode highlights a lack of independent oversight and verifiable records in AI deployment, posing risks to national security, finance and healthcare and necessitating a solution similar to aviation's flight recorders.
author: The Hill

title: Rep. Marlin Stutzman calls Trump's promotion of Stephen Miller a mistake
content: Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) on Sunday decried President Trump’s promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. “I come from the business world, just like President Trump does. And you know what? If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” Stutzman told…
summary: Rep. Marlin Stutzman, a Republican from Indiana, said on Sunday that President Trump's promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff was a mistake. He added that if a team takes a beating, it must fire people.
author: The Hill

title: Beto O'Rourke credits Democrats' past work for Texas “Blue Tsunami” midterm victory
content: NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke about how past efforts by him and other Democrats helped the party win big in Texas in the midterms.
summary: NPR's Rob Schmitz interviewed former Texas congressman Beto O'Rourke. O'Rourke said his and other Democrats' past efforts helped the party win big in Texas in the midterms.
author: NPR Politics

title: Dana White to meet Trump Monday after being offered White House press secretary job
content: UFC boss Dana White said he will meet with President Donald Trump on Monday regarding Trump’s Saturday announcement that he had offered White House press‑secretary duties to White, whom Trump described as a friend. The offer and upcoming meeting are the only details provided.
summary: President Donald Trump said Saturday he offered the White House press secretary job to UFC boss Dana White. Dana White said he will meet with Trump on Monday about the offer.
author: NPR Politics

title: Democrats target majorities in next Congress as Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff
content: Democrats are preparing for the next Congress, in which they will hold significant majorities in the House and Senate. At the same time, President Trump has indicated his intentions by promoting Stephen Miller to the position of Chief of Staff.
summary: Democrats plan for the next Congress where they will hold significant majorities in both chambers. President Trump signals his plans by promoting Stephen Miller as his new Chief of Staff.
author: NPR Politics

title: Hogan Gidley talks GOP post‑midterm strategy with NPR’s Ayesha Rascoe
content: NPR’s Ayesha Rascoe interviewed Hogan Gidley, a Republican consultant who served as White House Deputy Press Secretary during the first Trump administration, to discuss the GOP’s post‑midterm strategy, examining what went wrong and what lies ahead for the party.
summary: Ayesha Rascoe of NPR interviewed Hogan Gidley, a Republican consultant and former White House Deputy Press Secretary during the first Trump administration. They discussed what went wrong for the GOP and its post‑midterm strategy.
author: NPR Politics

title: NPR Moscow and Beijing correspondents discuss overseas reaction to U.S. midterm results
content: NPR’s correspondents based in Moscow and Beijing discuss how the United States’ midterm election results are being observed abroad, noting that the outcomes were closely followed in both Russia and China. Their conversation focuses on the perspectives and reactions within the countries they cover.
summary: NPR Moscow and Beijing correspondents discuss overseas reaction to U.S. midterm results.
author: NPR Politics

title: New Zealand election yields no clear winner; leaders to negotiate for weeks
content: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who will lead a caretaker government during upcoming negotiations, indicated that there is no clear winner in the recent election. He stated that he believes everyone is tired of politics and suggested taking a break for the next three weeks while leaders prepare for talks.
summary: The New Zealand election did not produce a clear winner, leading leaders to prepare for weeks of talks. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he will head a caretaker government and suggested a three‑week political break during negotiations.
author: NPR Politics

title: Sydney’s jacarandas blaze into flower, attracting photographers in October and November
content: Sydney’s jacaranda trees are in full bloom, covering the city in purple as the warmer weather arrives. In October and November the fast‑growing trees produce trumpet‑shaped blossoms that carpet the ground, attracting sightseers, photographers and onlookers who photograph the scene. The coverage also includes images from the Tesselaar tulip festival.
summary: Jacaranda trees in Sydney bloom in October and November, covering the streets with trumpet-shaped purple blossoms. The spectacle draws sightseers, photographers, and people taking photos of people taking photos.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Photographer Howard Loosemore releases new book on Australian fairywrens after 15 years
content: Photographer Howard Loosemore and several fellow photographers devoted 15 years to photographing every Australian fairywren species and its plumage. Their work appears in a newly released book that showcases the small, colourful lives of these birds.
summary: Howard Loosemore and a few photographer friends spent 15 years capturing every Australian fairywren species and plumage in vivid detail. The images have been published in a new book about the small and colourful lives of fairywrens.
author: Guardian Environment

title: COP31 climate summit in Turkey gathers over 190 nations as US absent
content: Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for the COP31 UN climate summit, with heads of government meeting for the next fortnight. The United States will be absent as the planet faces unprecedented human‑caused global heating, prompting the summit’s organizers to ask why the talks matter and what they are likely to achieve.
summary: Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for the COP31 climate talks. The United States will be absent while heads of government meet for the next fortnight amid unprecedented human‑caused global heating.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Australia to Host COP31 Negotiations in Antalya Amid Turkey Row
content:
The COP 31 climate summit has begun amid lingering tensions over its hosting arrangement. In 2021, Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, pledged to host the conference while he was still in opposition. However, complex rules delayed Australia’s bid, leading to a heated dispute with Turkey over the right to host. A final compromise placed Australia in charge of the negotiations, which will be conducted in Antalya, a city in Turkey.

The unresolved bitterness from the hosting row has left Australia’s role perceived as somewhat half‑hearted. Domestic media coverage of COP 31 has been noticeably quieter than in previous host countries. Although Albanese is scheduled to speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is expected to remain in the country only briefly.
summary: Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pledged to host COP31 in 2021, but a dispute with Turkey delayed the bid and led to a compromise that placed Australia in charge of negotiations in Antalya. Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, but is unlikely to stay long.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Labour set to slash UK EV targets despite Labour MP protests
content:
Labour ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s electric‑vehicle (EV) targets this week, a move that will relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs who are worried about the government’s commitment to the green agenda. The cuts are part of an emission‑reduction plan whose sales mandate is likely to be weakened, despite protests from MPs.

Louise Haigh, described as the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the revised plan after a crunch meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday, aimed at settling a long‑running dispute between the transport, energy and business departments.
summary: Ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government's electric vehicle targets this week, easing pressure on carmakers. Louise Haigh, described as the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalize the plan after a Downing Street meeting on Wednesday, despite concerns from many Labour MPs about the green agenda.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Study links Dinch plasticizer in food packaging to lower birth weight
content:
A peer‑reviewed study reports that exposure to a new generation of plasticizers, including the chemical Dinch, is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications. The research suggests these outcomes could lead to serious health problems later in life.

Din​ch, marketed as a “high safety” and nontoxic alternative to older phthalate plasticizers, is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union. The chemical also appears in children’s toys, medical devices, certain textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.
summary: A peer‑reviewed study found that exposure to the plasticizer Dinch, marketed as a “high safety” alternative and used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, is linked to lower birth weight. The same study reported that Dinch exposure is also associated with fetal development complications.
author: Guardian Environment

title: US datacenter demand fuels nearly 200 new fossil pipelines as Trump cuts safety rules
content:
A new review of federal records by the Environmental Integrity Project reveals that datacenter demand is driving a surge in fossil fuel pipeline projects. The report indicates that the Trump administration has simultaneously weakened regulations designed to protect lives and natural resources from disasters along these lines. Additionally, the pipelines are being constructed to satisfy natural gas export demand fueled by conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

Federal records identify nearly 200 proposed or active pipeline projects that would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km). This expansion occurs as the administration guts existing safety rules, linking increased datacenter energy needs to a growing infrastructure for fossil fuel transportation.
summary: US datacenter demand fuels nearly 200 new fossil pipelines as Trump cuts safety rules.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Beef industry drops teen climate lesson on cattle methane after rancher protest
content: A beef‑industry‑funded program that aimed to teach teenagers about the role of cattle’s methane emissions in the climate crisis has been quietly removed. The lesson, which originally explained how cows contribute to global heating, was scrapped after some ranchers protested and disputed the premise that cattle affect climate change. The episode reflects a continuing, decades‑long effort by the livestock sector to influence what U.S. children are taught about cows and their environmental impact.
summary: A beef industry‑funded effort to teach teenagers about cattle’s methane emissions and climate impact was quietly scrapped. The change came after some ranchers protested, disputing the premise that cows contribute to global heating.
author: Guardian Environment

title: ZEUS trial shows IL-6 blocker ziltivekimab lowers inflammation but not heart events
content:
Heart researchers unpack neutral findings from ZEUS, an anti‑inflammatory clinical trial. ZEUS is a global phase 3 study led by Mass General Brigham researcher Paul Ridker, M.D. The trial tested ziltivekimab, a drug that targets interleukin‑6 (IL‑6), a downstream inflammatory molecule commonly targeted by IL‑6 inhibitors used in autoimmune disorders.

The study found that while ziltivekimab effectively lowered IL‑6 levels, it did not reduce cardiovascular event rates compared with placebo. These neutral results suggest that targeting inflammation may be less straightforward than previously thought, even though inflammation is known to causally contribute to cardiovascular disease risk.
summary: Like cholesterol, inflammation causally contributes to the risk of cardiovascular disease, but findings from the clinical trial ZEUS indicate that the road to targeting inflammation may be less straightforward than once thought. ZEUS, a global phase 3 clinical trial led by Mass General Brigham researcher Paul Ridker, M.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Queen Mary study finds new treatment may cure hormonal hypertension after stopping meds
content: A study led by Queen Mary University of London reports that a new treatment may provide a lasting cure for some individuals with a common hormonal cause of high blood pressure, with effects persisting after medication is discontinued.
summary: A study led by Queen Mary University of London found that a new treatment could offer a lasting cure for some people with a common hormonal cause of high blood pressure. The effect may persist even after patients stop taking medication.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Mouse study: normal sleep may mask memory problems via ripple‑gate interneurons
content: A mouse study investigating how sleep stabilizes new memories identified specific interneurons that regulate the generation of ripples—brief bursts of electrical activity known to be essential for memory consolidation. The research, conducted by Min Xu and Wanling Peng and their team at the Institute of Neuroscience, Chinese Academy of Sciences, suggests these cells could serve as a genetic target for accessing neural circuits involved in cognitive disorders. The findings imply that sleep that appears normal may still conceal underlying memory problems.
summary: A mouse study testing how sleep stabilizes new memories identified interneurons that gate ripple bursts as a potential genetic target for circuits implicated in cognitive disorders. The research was led by Min Xu and Wanling Peng of the Institute of Neuroscience at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Potential driver of severe early-onset preeclampsia identified
content: Researchers have identified a potential driver of severe early‑onset preeclampsia, a condition that has puzzled physicians for more than two millennia. The disorder can appear as early as 20 weeks of gestation, causing sharply elevated blood pressure and endangering both mother and infant.
summary: Severe early-onset preeclampsia has puzzled doctors for more than 2,000 years. It can occur as early as 20 weeks of pregnancy, causing high blood pressure and endangering both mother and baby.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Financial incentives double quit rates for underserved smokers in national trial
content: A large national clinical trial that included Henry Ford Health found that providing financial incentives to medically underserved adults undergoing lung‑cancer screening almost doubled their smoking‑cessation rates. The study shows that monetary rewards can markedly increase quit success among this population.
summary: Financial incentives offered to people trying to quit smoking nearly doubled cessation rates among medically underserved adults undergoing lung cancer screening. The finding came from a large national clinical trial that involved Henry Ford Health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Single iron infusion boosts exercise capacity in HFpEF patients, study shows
content:
Investigators from the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute reported that a single iron infusion increased exercise capacity in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) who also have iron deficiency. The study’s results indicate that restoring iron stores may alleviate some of the physical limitations linked to this form of heart failure.

The findings were presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and were published concurrently in the journal Circulation.
summary: Investigators from the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute reported that a single iron infusion improved exercise capacity in people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and iron deficiency. The results were presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions and published simultaneously in Circulation.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Retatrutide cuts weight and eases knee osteoarthritis in Phase III trials
content: Two Northwestern University–led Phase III trials evaluated retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight‑loss drug, in participants with painful knee osteoarthritis who were overweight or had obesity. Across the combined trials, which enrolled more than 1,000 people, those receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost roughly one‑quarter of their body weight on average. The studies focused on the drug’s impact on weight reduction among individuals for whom everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs and standing from a chair are challenging.
summary: In two Northwestern University–led Phase III trials with more than 1,000 participants, the highest dose of retatrutide caused an average weight loss of about one‑quarter of body weight. The drug also eased pain and improved function for people with overweight or obese knee osteoarthritis.
author: Medical Xpress

title: City of Hope microbiome therapy shows promise in early trial to prevent bloodstream infections
content: Researchers at City of Hope and collaborators have introduced a first‑of‑its‑kind microbiome therapy that delivers 16 selected beneficial bacteria to patients receiving donor stem cell transplants for blood cancers. The approach aims to restore the microbiome and combat harmful pathogens, and early trial results indicate it may help prevent dangerous bloodstream infections.
summary: Researchers at City of Hope and collaborators have pioneered a new approach to preventing dangerous bloodstream infections in patients receiving donor stem cell transplants for blood cancers. The therapy delivers 16 carefully selected beneficial bacteria designed to restore the microbiome and fight harmful pathogens.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Five EU leaders urge closer EU-UK ties and clean‑energy cooperation ahead of summit
content: Five European leaders – the heads of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark – have urged closer relations with the United Kingdom ahead of an upcoming EU‑UK summit. In a letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Portuguese Prime Minister António Costa, they argued that deeper cooperation on clean‑energy initiatives would be mutually beneficial. The leaders’ appeal emphasizes the potential for joint progress in renewable‑energy projects as the summit approaches.
summary: The leaders of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark wrote a letter to Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa urging deeper cooperation on clean energy, saying it would benefit both sides. They also called for closer EU‑UK ties ahead of the anticipated EU‑UK summit.
author: Guardian Business

title: Bailiffs raid BYD offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp over JLR Defender clone claim
content: Bailiffs acting on behalf of Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp, seizing digital records, the Sunday Times reported. The seizure took place in August and precedes a court case this week that will examine whether BYD’s “Defender clone” infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s intellectual‑property rights over the Land Rover Defender. The raid is part of the legal dispute over the alleged copycat vehicle.
summary: In August, bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. They seized digital records ahead of a court case over whether BYD’s “Defender clone” infringes JLR’s intellectual property rights, the Sunday Times reported.
author: Guardian Business

title: Democrats win big House gains but have little ability to curb rising living costs
content:
Voters’ anxiety about rising prices has driven a political shift that analysts say could produce the largest swing toward Democrats since the Watergate era, giving the party its biggest House majority in almost forty years and its strongest Senate advantage since 2008. The surge is attributed to widespread concern over the cost of living, including gas, groceries, mortgages and healthcare.

According to the commentary, the newly empowered Democrats, who campaigned on restoring affordability, are likely to find limited options for easing these pressures over the next couple of years. The analysis suggests that immediate legislative action may not substantially reduce the financial strain on voters.

The observations are presented by Eduardo Porter, a journalist who covers economics and politics and publishes the newsletter Being There on Substack.
summary: Democrats win big House gains but have little ability to curb rising living costs.
author: Guardian Business

title: Study examines loss vs. gain phrasing in personalized retirement savings reminders
content: Private retirement savings are gaining attention in public debate. A common approach to encouraging contributions involves framing reminders either as a warning about what could be lost by not saving or as a highlight of the benefits of saving. Studies that compare these loss‑focused and gain‑focused messages have so far yielded mixed findings, leaving it unclear which phrasing more effectively increases individuals’ saving efforts. The ongoing uncertainty underscores the need for further research on personalized savings reminders.
summary: Private retirement savings are an increasingly important topic in public debate. Research on whether loss‑framed or gain‑framed reminder messages is more effective has produced conflicting results.
author: Phys.org

title: Tropical regions lose more bird species than other areas as cities expand
content: Tropical ecosystems are noted for their exceptionally high and exuberant diversity.  Across many branches of the tree of life, biodiversity rises sharply from the poles toward the tropics—a pattern described as the latitudinal diversity gradient.  Fossil evidence indicates that this gradient has been a persistent feature for millennia.
summary: Tropical ecosystems host the greatest biodiversity on Earth. The latitudinal diversity gradient is evident across many groups and fossil evidence shows it has existed for millennia.
author: Phys.org

title: Florida chimp sanctuary uses drone to feed ape as floods swell property
content: A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary, home to about 200 apes, used a drone this week to deliver food to one animal after heavy rain flooded the property. The organization reported that the apes remained safe and that the floodwater was receding significantly by Saturday.
summary: A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary delivered food by drone to one of its 200 apes after heavy rain swamped the property. The organization said the animals remained safe and the water was receding significantly on Saturday.
author: Phys.org

title: NASA seeks applicants for new astronaut class to expand Artemis moon program
content: NASA announced that it is now accepting applications for a new astronaut class. The selected astronauts will work on expanding the Artemis program, which aims to send crews to the Moon and develop a permanent lunar base.
summary: NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class. The astronauts will help grow the Artemis program and build a permanent lunar base.
author: Phys.org

title: Stupendously large primordial black holes ruled out as dark matter source
content: A new assessment has concluded that “stupendously large” primordial black holes cannot serve as a source of the universe’s dark matter, according to the headline. Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects thought to have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe, distinguishing them from the black holes that arise when massive stars collapse. Some theories had proposed that such exceptionally massive primordial black holes might account for a significant share of dark matter, but the latest ruling rejects that possibility.
summary: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe. Some theories suggested that “stupendously large” primordial black holes could account for a significant share of dark matter, but they have now been ruled out as a dark matter source.
author: Phys.org

title: Game theory guides SETI to prioritize timing over star selection
content: Scientists working with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence are applying game‑theoretic approaches to guide their observations, emphasizing the timing of searches over the specific locations. While earlier efforts such as Project Phoenix (2012‑2015) examined roughly 1,000 sun‑like stars for technosignatures, researchers now argue that when we listen may be more crucial than where we point our instruments.
summary: Scientists are applying game theory to improve SETI's search for technosignatures. They note that timing may be more crucial than which stars are observed, as Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 sun‑like stars between 2012 and 2015.
author: Phys.org

title: Largest known ground‑dwelling bird species identified from Liang Bua cave fossils
content: Researchers have identified a new, largest‑of‑its‑kind ground‑dwelling bird species from a leg bone discovered in 2009 within the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island, the same site where Homo floresiensis was found. The fossil, dated to roughly 190,000–120,000 years ago, was initially recognized as a bird bone, set aside and later reexamined.
summary: In 2009 researchers uncovered a 190,000–120,000‑year‑old leg bone in the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island. The bone was later identified as belonging to a new, largest‑of‑its‑kind ground‑dwelling bird species from the same cave as Homo floresiensis.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists map coral colony over 1.5 km on Cocos (Keeling) Islands, among world’s largest
content:
Scientists have mapped a coral colony that stretches roughly 100 buses in length. The colony extends more than 1.5 kilometres (0.93 miles) along the outer reef of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

Researchers say the size of this formation places it among the world’s largest known coral colonies ever recorded.
summary: Scientists map coral colony over 1.5 km on Cocos (Keeling) Islands, among world’s largest.
author: Phys.org

title: COP31 may show how climate summits can still deliver modest progress
content: No one expects COP31 to prevent climate disaster, yet the summit may demonstrate that international meetings can still achieve modest, meaningful progress.
summary: No one expects COP31 to solve the climate crisis. It could provide a small taste of how international meetings can still achieve meaningful progress.
author: New Scientist

title: 24‑hour fast boosts gut bacterium that aids intestinal regeneration after radiation
content: Scientists have found that a 24‑hour fast raises levels of a beneficial gut bacterium that promotes intestinal regeneration after radiation damage. The preclinical results suggest the possibility of developing treatments to protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without the need for patients to undergo fasting.
summary: Scientists found that a 24‑hour fast raises a beneficial gut bacterium that helps intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could lead to treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.
author: Science Daily

title: Daily 2–3 Cups of Coffee Linked to Lower Dementia Risk and Better Cognition
content: A study tracking participants for as long as 43 years found that consuming two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day was associated with a dramatically lower risk of dementia and with better cognitive functioning. The protective link persisted regardless of participants’ genetic risk, while no comparable association was observed for decaffeinated coffee.
summary: A study of up to 43 years found that drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was associated with a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning. The benefits were seen regardless of genetic risk, while decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.
author: Science Daily

title: High-dose flu shot linked to 55% lower Alzheimer's risk in seniors
content:
A new study from UTHealth Houston has found that a high‑dose influenza vaccine may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease in older adults. Researchers examined data from nearly 200,000 adults aged 65 and older.  

The analysis showed that those who received the high‑dose flu shot had a nearly 55 % lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s. This reduction is higher than the 40 % risk decrease previously linked to the standard‑dose vaccine. The findings suggest that a stronger flu vaccine could offer additional protective benefits for seniors against Alzheimer’s disease.
summary: Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that receiving a high-dose influenza vaccine was associated with a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. This reduction is greater than the approximately 40% risk reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds multi‑form cannabis users far more likely to have use disorder
content:
Scientists have identified a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction in a recent study of more than 17,700 adults in the United States. The research examined patterns of cannabis use across different consumption methods.

The study found that individuals who use cannabis in multiple forms—such as smoking, vaping, and edibles—exhibit dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms compared with those who primarily consume a single method. Nearly 67 % of multi‑form users met criteria for cannabis use disorder, whereas only 15 % of those who mainly consumed edibles did.
summary: Study finds multi‑form cannabis users far more likely to have use disorder.
author: Science Daily

title: Mysterious gas emissions and new fissures hint Mars may still be volcanically active
content: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures on Mars suggest the planet may not be geologically dead. Scientists say hot magma could still be active deep underground, creating hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy that might support microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
summary: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures on Mars suggest the planet may not be geologically dead. The findings indicate possible deep‑lying hot magma and hidden warmth that could provide chemical energy for microbial life beneath the surface.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find 1,000 cannabis seeds in 2,800‑year‑old Siberian Scythian tomb
content: Scientists studying a 2,800‑year‑old Siberian tomb uncovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical traces that indicate the ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating properties. The burial, which also contained evidence of elaborate rituals and animal sacrifices, provides the oldest directly dated archaeological proof of psychoactive cannabis use.
summary: Scientists investigating a 2,800‑year‑old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The find offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use and was surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds asteroid shape can change nuclear blast deflection effectiveness up to fivefold
content: Scientists report that a nuclear explosion could prevent a deadly asteroid from striking Earth, but new research warns that targeting the wrong side may backfire. The study shows an asteroid’s irregular shape can drastically alter its reaction to an X‑ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying by nearly fivefold depending on the impact angle.
summary: A nuclear explosion could be used to deflect a deadly asteroid threatening Earth. New research shows an asteroid’s irregular shape can cause deflection effectiveness to vary by almost five times depending on the angle of the X‑ray blast, meaning hitting the wrong side could lead to failure.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists discover quantum limit on electron tracking, could enable ultra-fast electronics
content: Scientists have identified a quantum limit that stops electrons from being measured with unlimited precision in both space and time. According to the researchers, this discovery could enable new control over chemical reactions and lead to electronics operating hundreds of thousands of times faster than current technology.
summary: Scientists have discovered a quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could enable manipulation of chemical reactions and the development of electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than current technology.
author: Science Daily

title: Ordnance Survey celebrates 225 years since first map, 1801 Kent map took decade
content: The 225th anniversary of the organisation’s first publication is an opportunity to celebrate its unique contribution to our sense of place In his one-paragraph short story, On Exactitude in Science, Jorge Luis Borges imagines an empire in which the level of cartographical ambition is so high that a map is made on a one-to-one scale with the imperial territory. The quest for perfect accuracy doesn’t end well. But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication. The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation, her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. During the course of the 19th century, the entirety of the British isles was meticulously mapped through fog, rain, wind and sun, in what was described as “a wild and arduous exercise”. The surveyors, armed with theodolites, measuring chains and notebooks, saw themselves as footsoldiers serving in the ranks of Reason as they brought intellectual order to the landscape.
summary: The Guardian editorial notes that Ordnance Survey is marking the 225th anniversary of its first publication. It recalls that the 1801 OS map of Kent required ten years to produce, driven by military concerns over a possible Napoleonic invasion.
author: Guardian Science

title: Baxdrostat shows blood pressure benefits lasting up to two years after use
content:
A new medication, baxdrostat, has shown unusually lasting effects on high‑blood‑pressure patients.  In a six‑ to 12‑month daily‑pill regimen, patients’ blood pressure improved, and the benefits persisted for up to two years after they stopped taking the drug.  

Doctors report that some patients no longer required any hypertension drugs and may have been cured of the condition, a result that has “stunned” clinicians.  The drug is said to reverse a common cause of high blood pressure, offering a potential long‑term solution for millions of people with the condition.
summary: Patients who took the daily pill baxdrostat for six to 12 months saw their blood pressure improve and the drug reversed a common cause of hypertension. The improvements persisted for up to two years after stopping the medication, with some patients no longer needing any hypertension drugs.
author: Guardian Science

title: Bininj rock shelter in Kakadu shows Namarrkon wielding lightning
content:
In a rock shelter in Kakadu National Park, the Bininj people have carved an image of Namarrkon, one of their most important creation ancestors. The carving shows Namarrkon’s flesh bleached away to reveal bone, stone axes fixed to his head, elbows, and knees, and a great band of lightning that extends from his ankles, over his head, and beyond.

Namarrkon’s journey from the coast to the Arnhem Land escarpment is believed to have shaped the surrounding landscape. In the great storms that sweep across the region during the wet season, the Bininj attribute the splitting of clouds, the thunder, the lightning, and the release of life‑giving rain to Namarrkon’s stone axes.

The depiction underscores the Bininj belief that Namarrkon’s power over thunder and lightning is integral to the creation and sustenance of their environment.
summary: Humans have always been awed by the power and beauty of lightning. How does the experience and understanding of it change in a warming world?

title: NASA Calls for New Generation of Astronauts to Live and Work on the Moon
content:
NASA has announced a call for a new generation of astronauts who could live and work on the moon. Applications are open until 3 December as part of the latest expansion of the Artemis program.  

The agency says successful candidates will help “shape humanity’s future in space” by building a lunar base and preparing for the first crewed missions to Mars.
summary: NASA has opened applications for a new generation of astronauts to live and work on the moon, with the deadline on 3 December. Successful candidates will help shape humanity's future in space as the agency builds a lunar base and prepares for the first crewed missions to Mars.

title: APOD features major fireball meteor captured over Italy on Nov 8 2026
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day for November 8, 2026 features a photograph taken on 14 November 2017 from a mountain pass in the Dolomite Alps of Italy. The image shows snowy, rugged peaks above the village of La Villa, Alta Badia, with the twilight sky rendered in soft pinkish hues. The constellation Ursa Major, including the Big Dipper asterism, is visible on the northern horizon.

During the camera’s exposure a bright fireball meteor crossed the sky from east to west, flashing above the village lights. The meteor was captured serendipitously in the same frame as the landscape. The event was reported widely across European skies, making it one of the most reported fireball occurrences recorded by the American Meteor Society and the International Meteor Organization.

Analysis of the meteor’s measured track over Germany indicates a trajectory consistent with an origin near the active radiant of the Northern Taurid meteor shower, which is associated with dust from Encke’s comet. The APOD entry credits the photograph to Ollie Taylor and lists Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, and Keighley Rockcliffe as authors and editors. The service is provided by ASD at NASA/GSFC, NASA Science Activation, and Michigan Tech.
summary: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 8 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

title: NASA launches $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge for U.S. schools
content:
NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge on Sunday during a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. The competition, launched as part of a Golden Age of Science, invites student teams from U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools to submit designs for the Moon Base. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that the agency is seeking students who can think creatively, work as a team, and address real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon, emphasizing that curiosity and the willingness to tackle hard problems are essential qualities for building what comes next.

The Moon Base is being developed in the lunar South Pole region, where astronauts will live, work, and explore. A permanent human presence on the Moon is described as paving the way for future crewed missions to Mars and requiring talent from various industries and backgrounds. Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, noted that the agency wants to leverage ingenuity and innovation to consider every need for explorers living and working on the lunar surface. He expressed anticipation for the fresh perspectives and bold ideas that students will bring to the project, stating that the Moon Base is ultimately for the next generation who will experience a world where humans remain on the Moon.

The multiphase challenge supports NASA’s commitment to cultivating the technical skills of tomorrow’s aerospace workforce. Student teams are tasked with designing innovative solutions across six specific categories: power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks, and astronaut safety. The challenge provides participants with an opportunity to develop skills necessary for careers in the space industry while helping to advance new concepts for Moon Base technologies.

Participants must register for the challenge through the NASA STEM Gateway, with registration open until January 25, 2027. The challenge addresses authentic environmental and mission design parameters for life and operations on the lunar surface. Deliverables reflect industry skills such as trade studies, concept proposals, and stakeholder briefings, allowing participants across technical, vocational, and various academic tracks to build career-relevant skills without requiring prior specialized engineering or technical experience.

Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters, described students as the next generation of explorers and innovators whose unique perspectives are key to envisioning a future away from Earth. The Office of STEM Engagement designed the challenge in collaboration with the Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. Complete competition details, eligibility requirements, and official rules are available at moonbasechallenge.org.
summary: Artist’s concept depicting astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems, and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at the Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. Credit: NASA On Sunday, NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida.

title: UV-Tracking Necklace Gem Alerts Wearer to High Sun Exposure During LA Heat
content:
During a relative’s outdoor party in August, temperatures in Los Angeles reached the 90s. The writer sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan, assuming protection from the heat. After about thirty minutes, the writer experienced exhaustion, dizziness, nausea, and general illness—symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

At the same time, a notification from an app linked to a $249 (later $149) UV‑tracking necklace called Gem, manufactured by The90, alerted the wearer that UV exposure had risen significantly. The alert coincided with the onset of the writer’s heat‑related symptoms.
summary: The author wore a Gem UV‑tracking necklace from The90, priced at $249 ($149 at time of publication), while attending a relative’s outdoor party in Los Angeles in August. The necklace’s app notified the author that UV exposure had risen sharply as they experienced heat‑exhaustion symptoms.

title: Apple iOS 27.3 beta hints at chatbot support for HomeView
content:
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta includes a flag for a “Conversational Apps” category, suggesting Apple may enable chatbot support on its HomeView smart‑home hub. The beta does not specify which apps could use the category, but the presence of the flag implies that AI chatbots such as ChatGPT or Claude could be added.

The same beta also introduces bidirectional audio routing and session‑management features, which a source identified as pdfu on X described as “still not fully wired up.” Additionally, Apple has added anti‑spoofing protection that will prompt users to authenticate with an iPhone after three failed attempts and will enforce a lockout mechanism.

title: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air hits lowest price since July
content:
Apple’s M5‑powered 13‑inch MacBook Air is now listed at $1,099.99, the lowest price it has reached since July. The discount represents a $200 reduction and is the second time the model has been offered at this level after the company’s summer price increases. The base configuration includes the M5 processor, 16 GB of RAM and a 512 GB SSD, and it is being sold at the reduced price by Amazon, Best Buy and B&H Photo in all color options.

When the 13‑inch Air launched in May, it typically sold for roughly $950 to $1,000, but price cuts have been uncommon since July, making the current offer notable. A larger 15‑inch MacBook Air, which adds a six‑speaker array and two extra GPU cores, is also discounted by $200 and is priced at $1,299.99 for the same 16 GB RAM/512 GB SSD configuration. The 15‑inch model is likewise available from Amazon, Best Buy and B&H Photo in most colors.

The article notes that, despite being more expensive than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air provides “better value” through double the RAM, a faster CPU with more cores, twice the storage, improved speakers, a backlit keyboard and a larger, higher‑resolution screen. Readers are directed to earlier reviews of the MacBook Neo and the M5 MacBook Air for additional context.

title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders sue AI music firm Suno over voice cloning
content:
Sun​o, an AI music company, is being sued in two separate actions. One suit is brought by a group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music, and the other by the publisher of several of Eminem’s major records. Both parties allege that Sun​o illegally generates music and lyrics that imitate the respective artists.

In the Presley case, the plaintiffs’ lawyers contend that Sun​o has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which prohibits an AI firm from cloning a singer’s voice. They further argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard‑work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for …”. The lawsuits claim the company’s technology infringes on the artists’ protected rights.
summary: Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists.
author: The Verge

title: British soldier court-martialed after refusing to remove SIM card, blackmailed
content:
An Estonian newspaper reported that British soldier Daniel Barton‑Kennedy ignored a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a location in Estonia about 90 miles west of the Russian border. After refusing the operational‑security measure, his phone was hacked, nude photographs were stolen and used to blackmail him.

Barton‑Kennedy was subsequently court‑martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pleaded guilty, was reduced in rank and sentenced to ten months’ detention.
summary: British soldier court-martialed after refusing to remove SIM card, blackmailed.
author: Ars Technica

title: Scientists study Great Zimbabwe iron furnaces to trace Bantu expansion impact
content:
Scientists continue to investigate how the Bantu expansion reshaped Africa, seeking evidence of the cultural and technological changes it brought. One focus of current research is the iron‑working expertise demonstrated by the ancient inhabitants of Great Zimbabwe, the capital of a prosperous southern‑African kingdom that flourished from roughly 1000 to 1700 AD.

Archaeologists have identified clusters of iron‑smelting furnaces near the stone ruins of Great Zimbabwe, now visible as mounds of rubble. At the nearby village of Mashava, about 25 miles northwest, fragments of furnace interiors retain the fingerprints of the workers who once smoothed the clay. Some furnaces measured nearly an adult’s arm span across and featured thick walls capable of containing temperatures above 2,100 °F, sufficient to melt iron ore. Unlike many contemporary furnaces that required manual bellows, these structures drew air in and expelled it through a chimney, eliminating the need for human labor and facilitating the production of tools such as hoes, axes and arrowheads.
summary: Scientists are still tracing how the Bantu expansion changed Africa. The iron‑smelting furnaces at Great Zimbabwe, a capital from 1000‑1700 AD, were large self‑ventilating structures that produced iron for hoes, axes and arrowheads without using bellows.
author: Ars Technica

title: Physicists use electrical noise to probe cuprate pseudogap
content: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. Read full article Comments
summary: Physicists Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University measured the faint electrical crackle from current flowing into a cuprate to study its pseudogap. Their recent Science study reports that the pseudogap involves missing electrons above the superconducting temperature, offering new clues to high‑temperature superconductivity.

title: Leaked docs reveal Cisco expanded Israeli military contracts amid Gaza war
content:
Leaked documents reveal that Cisco intensified its dealings with Israel’s military intelligence during the Gaza war, despite internal protests by workers over the company’s involvement. The tech conglomerate “leaped to shore up” its relationship with the Israeli agencies even as the firm faced criticism from its own staff.

A year into the conflict, Israel’s military intelligence networks experienced prolonged outages, multi‑hour system crashes and failed debugging mechanisms. These persistent technical problems eroded the confidence of the intelligence agencies in Cisco, one of their primary network providers.
summary: Leaked documents show Cisco increased its deals with Israel’s military intelligence during the Gaza war. The company sought to shore up the relationship despite worker protests and repeated network outages that had eroded Israeli confidence in its services.
